tokenRules.message: Hex color hardcoded. Use semantic tokens (var(--primary), var(--bg-surface), var(--text-default), ...).
RGB/HSL hardcoded. Use semantic tokens via var(--*).
Tailwind palette color. Use semantic webkit tokens (var(--primary), var(--text-default), var(--bg-surface), ...).
Raw Tailwind text size. Use a generated typography class (text-heading-md, text-body-sm, text-button-lg, ...).
Legacy/external color utility. Use semantic webkit tokens (var(--text-default), var(--bg-surface), ...).

bounce.useWhen: Playful attention bounce (scroll-down hints); use sparingly.

brand-marquee.useWhen: A strip of logos looping forever (client trust strips, framework strips). Apply to a track holding its row exactly twice, the duplicate aria-hidden, and set animation-duration ON THE ELEMENT from the mark count so every strip on a site moves at one speed rather than one duration — a var in this shorthand would resolve at :root and never see it. Pause it on hover and focus-within so a linked mark can be reached.

content-enter.useWhen: Content settling INSIDE a page that is already on screen — a loading window resolving, a filtered list swapping, a step changing. Never on first paint of a page whose own entrance is already running (use it after that entrance, or after a wire). Stagger a follower with --content-enter-delay.

fade-in.useWhen: Content or backdrop appearing in place (no directional origin).

fade-out.useWhen: Content or backdrop leaving in place (pair of fade-in).

flow-dash.useWhen: Flowing connection along an SVG connector stroke in a node-based / network diagram. Set a stroke-dasharray whose cycle divides 24 (e.g. 4 4) so the loop is seamless.

highlight-fade.useWhen: Row/item briefly highlighted after an update (recently changed).

page-enter.useWhen: A page arriving on a route change — on the CONTENT ZONE only, never the shell. The chrome is the same before and after, and sliding it announces a reload that did not happen. Key it on the route path so a component serving several paths still replays it. Nothing inside the page may animate on mount at the same time: the two run in lockstep and read as one element travelling on a diagonal.

ping.useWhen: One-off attention ring radiating from a small element (notification dot).

popup-scale-in.useWhen: Anchored overlays opening (dropdown, popover, tooltip, menu); set --popup-origin.

progress-indeterminate-short.useWhen: Indeterminate linear progress bar (secondary short sweep).

pulse.useWhen: Skeleton/placeholder opacity pulse while content loads.

shimmer.useWhen: Skeleton shimmer sweep while content loads.

slide-down.useWhen: Vertical disclosure expanding (accordion panel, expandable row).

slide-in-left.useWhen: Left-anchored panel entering (sidebar, navigation drawer). Wrap the v-if region in a Vue Transition with enter-active-class.

slide-out-left.useWhen: Left-anchored panel leaving (pair of slide-in-left; use as leave-active-class).

texture-wave-a.useWhen: One of the two crossing bands of a pixelate texture, travelling left. Set --texture-wave-shift on the element to one period of its banding measured along X, and overhang the element by that much on the side it travels toward, or the field uncovers mid-cycle.

texture-wave-b.useWhen: The counter-travelling band of that pair (pair of texture-wave-a; same --texture-wave-shift contract, opposite direction).

props.concept: text of a link or call-to-action

events.noEchoRule: Do not emit "<x>-change" when "update:<x>" exists — it is redundant; use v-model / @update:<x>.

surfaces.product: Product UI (the console and other apps). The default for components.
surfaces.marketing: The marketing site (azion.com): page sections, bands, brand and client assets.
surfaces.docs: The documentation site: doc page chrome, callouts, steps, on-this-page.

props.name: singleLine
props.doc: Keeps the prefix and the label on one line (no wrapping).

props.name: showCursor
props.doc: Shows a blinking terminal-style cursor after the label.

props.name: prefix
props.doc: Preset prefix rendered before the label; empty renders no prefix.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: The label text, rendered uppercase in the brand primary color.

overline.purpose: Overline is the short uppercase label set above a headline to name the section, panel or group it opens (the "eyebrow"). It renders its default slot in `.text-overline-md` in the brand primary color, optionally behind a preset code-style prefix (`//`, `<>`, `</>`) and followed by a blinking terminal-style cursor. It is purely presentational text with no interaction; the marketing headers (`section-title`, `hero-title`, `call-to-action`, `media-split`, `ticker`) and several page sections render their eyebrow (the `eyebrow` prop, or `label` on `ticker`) through it.
useWhen: Name a section, panel or column group with one or two words set above its headline.
Build a custom marketing header that must match the eyebrow treatment of `section-title` and `hero-title` (the `//` prefix and the blinking cursor).
Label a band inside a page section (a comparison group, a closing panel) with the same uppercase code-style mark.
avoidWhen: The header has a headline, description and actions → use `section-title` (or `hero-title` for the hero), which already renders its `eyebrow` through Overline.
The text is a status, count or category attached to an item → use `tag` or `badge`.
The text is the heading itself → use a real heading element; Overline renders a `div` and is not a heading.
The text is a keyboard shortcut → use `kbd`.
The text is a field label → use `label`.
related: section-title` — the framed section header; renders its `eyebrow` as an Overline with `prefix="//"` and `show-cursor`.
hero-title` — the hero copy block; renders its `eyebrow` as an Overline closed by the cursor, with `single-line` turned off.
tag` — a compact label attached to an item, not a heading companion.
badge` — a compact count or status indicator.
bestPractices: Keep the label to one or two words: it is set uppercase and, with the default `single-line`, never wraps.
Turn `single-line` off only when the label can be longer than its container (narrow columns, translated copy); the label then wraps under `text-pretty`, which avoids a lone word on the last line.
Use a `prefix` from the preset set only (`//`, `<>`, `</>`); the prefix is decorative and hidden from screen readers (`aria-hidden="true"`), so never put meaning in it.
Use `show-cursor` for one eyebrow per view at most; the blink stops under reduced motion.
Keep the semantic heading in the element after the Overline; the Overline itself carries no heading role.

props.doc: Which side of the label the icon sits on. `leading` is a glyph that names the action; `trailing` is a glyph that points at where it goes.

props.name: animated
props.doc: Nudges a trailing icon along its axis on hover. Off by default; marketing CTAs opt in.

props.name: href
props.doc: When set, renders as a link (`<a>`).

props.name: target
props.doc: Link target when `href` is set.

props.name: type
props.doc: Native button type. `submit` lets the control submit its form; `disabled` and `loading` still block it. Ignored when `href` is set.

slots.name: prefix
slots.notes: A mark drawn before the label, ahead of a leading `icon`. It stays first when `iconPosition="trailing"`, so a brand mark and a trailing chevron can share one control.

button.purpose: Interactive control for user actions. Lives at `packages/webkit/src/components/actions/button/`.
useWhen: Trigger an action that needs a visible text label: in a form, dialog footer, toolbar or page header.
Mark the main action of a view with `kind="primary"` and the lesser ones with `secondary`, `outlined` or `transparent`.
Submit or reset a form with `type="submit"` / `type="reset"`.
A call to action that navigates: set `href` (and `target`) and it renders as an anchor with the same look.
avoidWhen: The control is icon-only → use `icon-button`.
One default action with related alternatives in an attached menu → use `split-button`.
A standalone navigation link with a trailing icon and a ghost hover → use `link`.
The single AI or highlight entry point that must stand out from every other action → use `button-highlight`.
related: icon-button` — icon-only counterpart with the same sizes and a required `ariaLabel`; its `transparent` kind matches this one.
split-button` — joins a Button to a chevron menu of related actions.
button-highlight` — the same prop surface without `kind`, drawn with the brand gradient and a rotating glow rim.
mini-button` — compact text action with a brand-colored trailing icon for dense cards and tables.
toggle-group` — a group of mutually exclusive options, not a single action.
bestPractices: Keep one `kind="primary"` per view or region; use `danger` only for destructive actions.
Set `loading` while the action resolves: it swaps the icon for a spinner, sets `aria-busy` and suppresses `click`, so the handler needs no extra guard.
Use `iconPosition="leading"` for a glyph that names the action and `"trailing"` for one that points where it goes; add `animated` only on marketing CTAs with a trailing icon.
Put brand or product marks in the `prefix` slot; `icon` takes a PrimeIcons class.
label` is required and is the accessible name; never pass an empty string to get an icon-only control.

button-highlight.purpose: Visually emphasized action trigger built on a brand-accent gradient with a continuously rotating multicolor glow rim behind the surface (ported from the `azion-console-kit` Copilot button). Use it to draw attention to a primary AI / highlight flow that needs to stand out from a regular `Button`. One visual treatment (the gradient + glow); same prop surface as `Button` minus the `kind` axis.
useWhen: The single entry point to an AI assistant or highlight flow (for example "Ask Azion") that must stand out from the actions around it.
A headline action in a header or marketing band where a primary `button` would blend in.
avoidWhen: A regular primary or secondary action → use `button`.
An icon-only control → use `icon-button`.
A default action with related alternatives in a menu → use `split-button`.
related: button` — the default action control; adds `kind`, `iconPosition`, `animated`, `type` and a `prefix` slot that this component does not have.
icon-button` — icon-only action when there is no room for a label.
bestPractices: Use at most one per view; the glow loses its meaning when it repeats.
Keep the label short and verb-led, and pair it with a leading `icon` (for example `pi pi-sparkles`).
It always renders `type="button"`; use `button` with `type="submit"` to submit a form.
disabled` and `loading` both hide the glow, apply the disabled surface and suppress `click`.
The glow stops under reduced motion, so never use it to convey state.

mini-button.purpose: Compact text action with an optional trailing external-link icon and a ghost hover surface. Use for secondary CTAs in dense layouts (cards, tables, toolbars) where a full `Button` is too heavy. Differs from `navigation/link` by using default body text color and a brand-colored icon.
useWhen: A short secondary CTA ("Learn more") inside a card, feature tile or table where a full `button` is too heavy.
A marketing link that reads in body text color with a brand-colored icon.
avoidWhen: A standalone navigation link in product UI (a domain, a repository, a docs page) → use `link`.
The main action of a section → use `button`.
A link inside a sentence → use a plain anchor with the text-link class.
related: link` — same anatomy (label, trailing icon, ghost hover) in link color, with a `small` size; the default for standalone links.
button` — full action control with kinds, loading and a button element.
bestPractices: Always set `href`; the default `'#'` is a placeholder and the control always renders as an anchor.
Replace the `'Learn More'` default `label` with text that says where the link goes.
Keep the default `pi pi-external-link` icon for off-site targets with `target="_blank"` (`rel="noopener noreferrer"` is added for you); set `showIcon` to false otherwise.
Only `large` and `medium` sizes exist.

props.doc: Text copied to the clipboard on activation.

props.name: ariaLabel
props.doc: Accessible name while idle. Empty uses the locale catalog (`Copy`).

props.name: copiedLabel
props.doc: Accessible name while the copied state is shown. Empty uses the locale catalog (`Copied`).

props.name: kind
props.doc: Visual variant forwarded to `IconButton`.

props.name: size
props.doc: Size token forwarded to `IconButton`.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Disables interaction and applies disabled tokens.

events.name: copy
events.notes: Emitted after a successful clipboard write with the copied value.

copy-button.purpose: Icon-only control that copies a string to the clipboard and briefly confirms success. Composes `IconButton` for visuals and interaction tokens, and `Tooltip` for its name: an icon-only button is silent to a pointer user until hovered, so the glyph is always labelled on hover/focus. The tooltip text is the same string as the accessible name — `ariaLabel` while idle, `copiedLabel` for the two seconds after a write — so the confirmation is seen as well as announced. It is suppressed with `disabled`.
useWhen: Next to a value the user will paste elsewhere: an ID, a domain, a token, a CLI command.
Inside key/value rows, terminal mocks and code samples that need a one-click copy.
avoidWhen: The action is anything other than copying → use `icon-button`.
A labelled "Copy" action in a form or dialog footer → use `button`.
A full code sample with its own copy control → use `code-block`.
related: icon-button` — the control it composes; `kind` and `size` are forwarded to it.
tooltip` — composed to show `ariaLabel` and then `copiedLabel` on hover and focus.
code-block` — already embeds a copy-button for its content.
bestPractices: Pass the exact text in `value`; an empty `value` makes the click a no-op.
Localize `ariaLabel` and `copiedLabel`: each is both the accessible name and the tooltip text.
Listen to `copy` for analytics or a toast; it fires only after the clipboard write succeeds.
The click stops propagation, so it is safe inside clickable rows and cards.
Keep the `transparent` / `small` defaults in dense rows.

props.name: options
props.type: ToggleGroupOption[]` (`{ label?: string | number; value?: string | number; disabled?: boolean }`)
props.doc: Segmented choices shown as a mutually exclusive group.

props.name: ariaLabel
props.doc: Accessible name when no visible group label is associated.

props.name: defaultValue
props.doc: Initial selection when `v-model` is not set.

props.name: size
props.doc: Size token, on the same 28 / 32 / 40 rhythm every other control uses.

props.name: fluid
props.doc: Stretches the group to its container and lets the options share that width.

toggle-group.purpose: ToggleGroup is a connected group of buttons that picks exactly one value out of a small set of related options, with a selection indicator that slides to the active segment. It renders as a `radiogroup` whose segments are `radio` buttons, is driven by an `options` array plus `v-model`, and works uncontrolled through `defaultValue`. It differs from `tabs`, which switches between content panels it owns: a segmented button only holds the chosen value and leaves rendering what that value means to the consumer.
useWhen: Switch in place between two to five related modes, views or ranges (a time range, a list/grid view, a filter scope) where exactly one is always active.
Offer a compact single choice in a toolbar or a card header where a radio list would take too much room.
Show a choice that is currently unavailable as a locked segment (`disabled` option) instead of hiding it.
avoidWhen: The choice switches between content panels that belong to the control → use `tabs`.
The choice is a form field with a label, helper text or validation → use horizontal `field`s with a `radio-button`, or `Field.Label` choice cards when each option needs a description.
The value is a binary on/off setting → use `switch` (in a horizontal `field` inside a form).
The user can pick more than one option → use `checkbox` (in a horizontal `field`).
The control triggers an action instead of holding a value → use `button` or `split-button`.
related: tabs` — tabs that own their panels; reach for it when each option reveals its own content region.
field` — a horizontal `Field` with a `radio-button` is the form-field single choice with label and description; a `Field.Label` choice card when each option carries a title and description.
switch` — a single boolean toggle.
button` — a lone action; the segments here hold a value instead of firing one.
bestPractices: Keep labels to one or two words: segments never wrap (`whitespace-nowrap`) and long labels truncate.
Give every option a unique `value`; values are coerced to strings and used as the list key and the selection identity, so duplicates collide.
Pass `ariaLabel` whenever no visible label names the group.
Use `fluid` to make the group fill a narrow container and share its width across segments, instead of styling the width at the call site.
Bind `v-model` when the selection lives in the parent; use `defaultValue` only to seed an uncontrolled group.

icon-button.purpose: Interactive control for user actions. Lives at `packages/webkit/src/components/actions/icon-button/`.
useWhen: Compact actions in toolbars, table rows, card headers and overlay close controls where the glyph is widely understood (close, refresh, delete, more).
Swapping between two icons in place (copy to check, show to hide), with `iconTransition` animating the change.
An icon-only link: set `href` and it renders as an anchor.
avoidWhen: The action needs a visible label → use `button`.
Copying a value to the clipboard → use `copy-button`, which already wires the icon swap, the tooltip and the `copy` event.
Choosing one of a few mutually exclusive options → use `toggle-group`.
related: button` — labelled counterpart; sizes line up and its `text` kind matches `transparent` here.
copy-button` — IconButton plus Tooltip with the clipboard write built in.
tooltip` — wrap an IconButton to show its name on hover and focus.
split-button` — uses an IconButton as its chevron menu toggle.
bestPractices: ariaLabel` is required and is the only accessible name; describe the action ("Delete domain"), not the glyph ("Trash").
Wrap it in `tooltip` when the glyph is not self-evident, so pointer users see the name screen readers hear.
Use `kind="transparent"` in dense rows and toolbars; keep `primary` for a lone emphasized action.
Set `iconTransition` only when `icon` changes at runtime; with a static icon it adds nothing.
Use `iconClass` for glyph-level tweaks instead of styling the root.

props.name: label
props.doc: Visible label text on the primary command button.

props.name: icon
props.doc: PrimeIcons class for the primary button's leading icon.

props.name: model
props.doc: Actions rendered as rows in the attached overlay menu.

props.name: kind
props.doc: Visual variant applied to both joined segments.

props.name: size
props.doc: Size token; affects height, padding, and typography.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Disables both segments and prevents the menu from opening.

props.name: loading
props.doc: Shows a spinner on the primary button and takes the disabled status: both segments are disabled and the menu cannot open while it resolves.

props.name: updateLabelOnSelect
props.doc: When true, selecting a menu action updates the primary button's label and icon to mirror that action and marks it as selected in the menu. Opt-in; the mirrored action is also reported as the primary `click`'s second argument, so the consumer decides what each segment does.

events.name: click
events.notes: Fired by the primary command button on activation. `item` is the action currently mirrored on the primary segment when `updateLabelOnSelect` is on, otherwise `null`. Never fires while `disabled` or `loading`.

events.name: item-click
events.notes: Fired when a menu action is selected. `event` is the pointer/keyboard event that activated the option; `item` is the matched `model` entry. The menu cannot open while `disabled` or `loading`, so it never fires in those states.

split-button.purpose: A primary command button visually joined to a chevron toggle that opens an overlay menu of related actions defined by a `model` array. The primary button runs the default action; the joined toggle composes `navigation/dropdown` to present the remaining actions. Opt into `updateLabelOnSelect` to have the primary segment mirror the last-chosen menu action (label + icon), turning the control into a "default is the last selection" pattern; the primary `click` then reports that mirrored action as its second argument, so a single handler can run whichever action is active. Use it when one action is the default and related actions belong in an attached menu; for a single action use `Button`, and for a standalone menu use `DropdownMenu`.
useWhen: One default action with a few related alternatives (Save and Save as draft, Deploy and Deploy to staging).
A "repeat the last choice" control: set `updateLabelOnSelect` so the primary segment mirrors the last action picked.
avoidWhen: A single action → use `button`.
A menu with no default action → use `dropdown`.
Picking one of a few visible, mutually exclusive options → use `toggle-group`.
related: button` — the primary segment; `kind` here is limited to `primary`, `secondary` and `outlined`.
dropdown` — the overlay menu the toggle composes; use it alone when there is no default action.
icon-button` — the chevron toggle segment.
bestPractices: Give every `model` entry a stable `value`; without one the `label` identifies the action, so renaming it changes what handlers receive.
Handle the default action in `@click` and the menu actions in `@item-click`; both receive `(event, item)`.
With `updateLabelOnSelect`, read the second argument of `click` (the mirrored item, `null` until one is picked) to run whichever action is active.
Set `loading` while the action runs: it disables both segments and keeps the menu closed.
Disable a single action with `disabled: true` on its model entry instead of removing it, so the menu does not shift.

chart.purpose: A cartesian chart — lines, areas and bars over one category axis — composed from parts the consumer places by hand. The root owns the data model (series + labels), the scales, the hover/keyboard state and the loading / empty / error surface; each part (`Chart.Grid`, `Chart.Axis`, `Chart.Line`, `Chart.Area`, `Chart.Bar`, `Chart.Crosshair`, `Chart.Tooltip`, `Chart.Legend`) reads that state through context, so the consumer wires nothing. Rendering is in-house SVG and every color comes from the `--chart-*` role, so a chart re-themes with no per-theme code and adds no charting dependency.
useWhen: A measure over time — requests, threats, bandwidth per bucket — as one or more lines or areas.
Comparing magnitudes across ordered categories — top countries, attack families — as vertical or horizontal bars.
Parts of a total over time — allowed / blocked / logged — as stacked areas or stacked bars.
Any chart that must read the same as Azion Console Real-Time Metrics: crosshair, one tooltip listing every series, legend toggles, totals.
avoidWhen: A single headline number with a delta → use `stat-tile`.
Share of a small whole (six slices or fewer) with the total in the center → use `donut-chart`.
More than about seven classes that all carry meaning → use `table`; color stops separating past the six series slots.
Two measures on different scales → two charts side by side; this component never draws a second value axis.
related: chart-card` — the box a dashboard chart sits in: title, description, controls, drag and resize.
donut-chart` — part-to-whole at a glance, sharing this chart's palette, legend and states.
stat-tile` — one figure with a delta and a sparkline, for a KPI row above the charts.
table` — the exact numbers; a chart's own table view is the accessible twin, a `table` is the primary surface.
bestPractices: Pass series in a stable order: the slot follows the series position, so color follows the entity. A filter that hides a series keeps the others' colors.
Keep one value axis. Index two measures to a common base or split them into two charts.
Let the legend carry identity for two or more series; a single series needs no legend, its title names it.
Mark a series whose color means a state (blocked, error rate) with `color: 'danger'` and never reuse a status color as series 4.
Color a series that counts one severity level with `color: 'severity-critical'` (`-high`, `-medium`, `-low`, `-info`) so stacked bars and legends match the `SeverityTag` in the table below the chart.
Keep filters and the time range in one row above the dashboard, never inside a chart.
While data reloads, set `refetching` so the previous render holds at reduced opacity instead of flashing a skeleton.

chart-card.purpose: The box a dashboard chart lives in: a header with the title, the description and a controls zone, a content area padded or flush, an optional footer, and two optional handles that let the person move the card and resize it on a dashboard grid. The span (grid columns) and height are two-way models applied through custom properties, so the consumer's grid lays cards out with no script, and the reorder state stays with the page that owns the grid.
useWhen: Every chart on a metrics dashboard, so title, description, menu and size read the same everywhere.
A dashboard the person arranges: drag a card to reorder it, drag a corner to make it wider or taller.
avoidWhen: A KPI figure → use `stat-tile`, which is its own surface.
A general content card with no chart → use `card`.
A chart inline in a page section with its own heading → render `chart` alone.
related: chart`, `donut-chart` — what goes inside the content area; a chart inside a card takes its accessible name from the card title.
card` — the general-purpose card; ChartCard shares its surface tokens.
dropdown` — the "More options" menu (Copy query, Export CSV) composed into the controls zone.
bestPractices: Put the aggregation tag (Sum, Average) and the variation tag in `ChartCard.Controls`, before the menu.
Keep filters and the time range above the grid, never inside a card.
Use `flush` content for a plot that should run edge to edge, padded for everything else.
Give the page's grid `--chart-grid-columns` per breakpoint so a 6-column card never overflows a 1-column phone layout.
Persist `span` and `height` with the dashboard layout; they are plain numbers.

donut-chart.purpose: A part-to-whole chart drawn as a ring (donut) or a disc (pie): one slice per series, the total in the center, a legend beside it. It shares the cartesian chart's data model, palette, legend behavior and loading / empty / error surface, so a dashboard reads as one system. Each slice is the sum of its series values, so a time series passes straight in as its share of the range.
useWhen: Share of a small whole at a glance: top countries by blocked threats, traffic by protocol, cache hit versus miss.
A dashboard card where the total is the headline and the split is the context.
avoidWhen: Comparing close values or more than six slices → use `chart` with horizontal bars; angles are hard to compare.
Two slices → use `stat-tile` with the ratio; a two-slice pie says less than the number.
Change over time → use `chart`.
related: chart` — the cartesian sibling; same series model, so a dataset moves between them without reshaping.
chart-card` — the box a dashboard donut sits in.
stat-tile` — the total alone, with a delta.
bestPractices: Keep it to six slices or fewer; the seventh and beyond fold into Other automatically.
Order series by size so the largest slice starts at the top.
Use the center for the total and let hover or focus swap it to the active slice.
Pair it with the bar form of the same data when exact ranks matter (the console's country pie plus ordered bar).

props.doc: A rise is bad for this metric; flips the delta between success and danger.

stat-tile.purpose: A KPI tile: a label, one big figure that counts up into place with an optional muted unit, an optional delta `Tag` against a named period, and an optional sparkline that bleeds to the tile's edges along its bottom. The delta reads good or bad for the metric, not merely up or down: `inverse` flips the polarity for metrics where a rise is bad (threats, errors, latency). A row of tiles sits above a dashboard's charts; without a `trend` the tile is the figure alone, the shape a usage strip uses.
useWhen: The headline numbers of a dashboard: total requests, blocked threats, cache hit ratio, error rate.
A single value whose change matters more than its history; the sparkline adds the shape of that history.
avoidWhen: The history itself is the point → use `chart`.
A share of a whole → use `donut-chart`.
Marketing figures on a site band → use `big-numbers`.
related: chart` — the full history behind a tile.
chart-card` — the box for a chart; a tile is its own small surface and does not sit in one.
big-numbers` — the marketing figure band, with no delta and no live data.
spark-chart` — the sparkline the tile draws its `trend` with; use it alone for a trend beside a number in a list or table.
tag` — the delta renders as a `Tag`; the empty band's "No data" is a `Tag` too.
divider` — carries the "No data" `Tag` across the empty band.
bestPractices: Name the comparison period in `deltaLabel` ("vs previous 24 hours"); a bare percentage is ambiguous.
Set `inverse` on every metric where a rise is bad, so a growing threat count reads as a regression.
Keep the label in sentence case with no trailing colon.
Put the unit in `unit` ("GB", "ms", "%"), not inside `formatValue`, so it reads muted beside the figure.
Leave `trend` out for a strip of figures with no history; the tile then has no chart band.
Give the sparkline the same buckets as the chart below it, about twelve points.

bar-list.purpose: A ranked list of named values: each row is a tinted bar whose length is the value against the largest one, with the name inside the bar and the formatted value in a right-aligned column. It reads as a list, not a chart — no axes, no grid — so it suits top-N breakdowns inside a card, where a horizontal `chart` would spend its width on an axis gutter.
useWhen: Top-N breakdowns inside a card: top paths, top countries, top user agents, top rules triggered.
A ranking where the name matters as much as the size, and names are long enough to need the bar's full width.
Rows that lead somewhere — a filtered view of that path or country — via `href` or `item-click`.
avoidWhen: Several series per category, or values over time → use `chart`.
A share of a whole where the parts sum to 100% → use `donut-chart`.
One value against a limit (quota, usage) → use `progress`.
related: chart` — horizontal bars with an axis, for comparing several series per category.
donut-chart` — the share view of the same breakdown when the parts sum to a whole.
chart-card` — the box a BarList sits in on a dashboard.
bestPractices: Keep it to about ten rows; fold the tail into an "Other" row in the data rather than scrolling.
Leave `sort` on `descending` for rankings; use `none` only when the order itself carries meaning (pipeline steps, weekdays).
Pass the same `formatValue` as the chart beside it so a number reads the same in both.
Give interactive rows a destination the user expects — a filtered view of that item — not a detail drawer of the whole list.

spark-chart.purpose: A word-sized chart: one series drawn as an area, a line or bars, with no axes, grid, legend or tooltip, filling the width of its container at a fixed height. It shows the shape of a recent history next to a number — in a stat tile, a table row or a ticker card — where a full `chart` would be too much.
useWhen: The shape of a metric's recent history beside its current value: requests in the last hour, latency over the day.
Rows of comparable items, each with its own trend: one SparkChart per row of a list or table.
The trend inside a `stat-tile`, which draws its `trend` through this component.
avoidWhen: The reader needs exact values, a time axis or several series → use `chart`.
A ranking across categories → use `bar-list`.
Up/down status over discrete periods → use `tracker`.
related: stat-tile` — the KPI tile that renders its sparkline with SparkChart.
chart` — the full history with axes, tooltip and legend.
tracker` — a strip of status blocks rather than a measured shape.
bestPractices: Pair it with the number it describes; a spark alone has no scale and says nothing exact.
Use the same buckets as the chart behind it, about twelve to thirty points.
Leave `fromZero` off for prices and latencies, where the shape matters more than the magnitude; turn it on for counts that are meaningful from zero.
Give it an `ariaLabel` only when it stands without a nearby number; otherwise keep it decorative.

tracker.purpose: A status strip: one block per period — a day, an hour, a deployment — colored by its severity, with a readout of the period's label on hover or keyboard focus. It shows the history of a state at a glance (uptime, health checks, build results), where a `chart` would plot a measure.
useWhen: Uptime and availability history: ninety days of a service, a region or an origin.
Pass/fail history: health checks, scheduled jobs, deployments.
Any discrete sequence where each period has one state and the pattern of failures matters.
avoidWhen: A measured value over time → use `chart` or `spark-chart`.
The current state of one thing → use `status-indicator`.
A ranking across categories → use `bar-list`.
related: status-indicator` — the current state; a Tracker is that state's history.
spark-chart` — a measured trend rather than a sequence of states.
chart-card` — the box a Tracker sits in, with the uptime figure in its header.
bestPractices: Write each `label` as period plus state ("Nov 3 · Partial outage"), so the readout stands alone.
Leave periods with no data without a severity; they render neutral rather than pretending to be healthy.
Keep the period count fixed for a given view (90 days, 24 hours) so strips stacked in a list line up.
Put the summary figure (99.98% uptime) beside the strip; the strip shows where, the figure shows how much.

chip` — interactive/removable token.

severity-tag.purpose: SeverityTag labels an item with its place on an ordered severity scale: critical, high, medium, low or info. The level reads from a four-bar glyph, where the filled bars count the level, and from the label, so two levels never depend on colour alone to differ. It differs from `tag`, whose `severity` prop is a colour tone (success, warning, danger) with no order between values.
useWhen: Show how severe an alert, finding, detection, incident or vulnerability is, in a table cell, a list row or a detail header.
Rank items on a fixed five-step scale where critical and high must stay visibly distinct.
avoidWhen: The value is an outcome or a status with no order (allowed, blocked, healthy) → use `tag`.
The value is a count or a one-word indicator on an icon or avatar → use `badge`.
The user can select or remove the value (a severity filter) → use `chip`.
related: tag` — a toned status or category label; use it for outcomes and states, not for an ordered level.
badge` — a dense count or short-label indicator.
chip` — an interactive or removable token, for severity filters.
bestPractices: Keep the default label (the level name) so the text always names the level; override `label` only to translate it.
Use one SeverityTag per row, in its own column, so the glyphs line up and the scale reads down the column.
Do not pair the tag with a toned `tag` for the same level; the glyph and the ramp already carry it.

badge.purpose: Badge is a compact, non-interactive indicator that surfaces a numeric count or a very short status label with severity-based color coding. Use it to draw attention to a small piece of state — an unread count, a quantity, a short status word — and it is commonly overlaid on icons, avatars, or buttons. It differs from its sibling `tag`: `tag` is a labelled status/category chip (optional leading icon, optional pill shape, masked surfaces), whereas `badge` is a denser count/short-label indicator with fully filled severity surfaces and no icon affordance.
useWhen: Surface a numeric count or a very short status label attached to another element (a bell with unread count, a status dot with a label).
Convey severity through `kind` (neutral / success / danger / …) with a fully filled surface.
avoidWhen: The label is user-removable or selectable → use `chip`.
It is a labelled category/status with an optional leading icon or pill shape → use `tag`.
related: tag` — labelled status/category chip with optional icon and pill shape; use when the label is descriptive, not a count.
chip` — interactive/removable token; use when the user can select or dismiss it.
bestPractices: Keep the content to a count or a 1–2 word label; longer text belongs in `tag`.
Drive color from `kind`, never a hardcoded color or a raw palette class.

brand.purpose: The Azion brand logo, rendered as an inline SVG lockup. A single `kind` prop selects the lockup: `default` (the AZION wordmark) for standard surfaces, `reduced` (the "A" glyph) for compact headers and tight spaces, and `extended` (the AZION wordmark with the "move to the edge technologies®" tagline) for marketing-oriented layouts. It consolidates the loose `@aziontech/webkit/svg/azion/*` assets — which remain individually importable — behind one component.
useWhen: The Azion logo in a header, navigation bar, footer, sign-in screen or product mockup.
kind="reduced"` where space is tight (collapsed sidebar, mobile header).
kind="extended"` in marketing layouts that carry the tagline.
avoidWhen: A customer or partner logo → use `logo-wall`.
A person's or organization's picture → use `avatar`.
A decorative product graphic → use `illustration`.
related: site-nav` and `site-footer` — compose Brand for the site chrome.
avatar` — the picture or initials of a user, not the product mark.
logo-wall` — third-party company marks.
bestPractices: Choose the lockup with `kind` and the height with `size` (16 / 24 / 32 px); do not pass width or height classes, the width follows the lockup's aspect ratio.
Do not recolor or rebuild the SVG; use the component so every surface shows the same mark.
For a home link, wrap Brand in an anchor; its `role="img"` and accessible name "Azion" give the link its name.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: The live content, teleported into the frame's viewport `iframe` once it is ready. Renders client-side only.

browser-frame.purpose: A browser window that renders live webkit components inside a viewport of its own, so a page or story can show a real screen at a real device size — desktop, tablet or mobile — and resize it by hand. The default slot is teleported into an internal `iframe`, which gives the content a true width × height viewport: CSS breakpoints fire against the frame's simulated width, viewport units resolve against its simulated height, and content taller than the viewport scrolls inside it like a page. When the simulated width is wider than the space available, the frame scales the whole viewport down to fit instead of clamping it. The chrome's window dots, address and size readout are decoration; its one control is a copy button inside the address bar, and the frame's other controls are the resize handles on its right edge, bottom edge and bottom-right corner.
useWhen: Showing a real screen — a site band, a console page, a template — built from webkit components, at a device size you choose.
Letting a reader drag a layout from desktop to tablet to mobile to see how it responds, in Storybook or on a documentation page.
Pinning a composed example to a device size (`v-model:width` + `v-model:height`) so a story or page always shows the tablet or mobile layout.
Showing that a result lives at a URL — a deployed site, a preview link — by setting `address`.
avoidWhen: For a static screenshot or clip in documentation → use `doc-frame`.
For third-party content loaded from another origin → use `embed`.
For a mock of the Azion console's own shell on a marketing band → use the console shell mockup the page composes; it draws the console chrome and staggers its parts.

For content whose layout depends on an overlay (`dialog`, `drawer`, a dropdown panel) or a JS breakpoint composable — those still read the outer page (see States), so the frame cannot show them at the simulated size.
For a framed page section or grid cell → use `frame-box`.
related: doc-frame` — the documentation figure frame for stills and clips; no live viewport.
embed` — a titled `iframe` for another origin's document; `browser-frame` renders our own components.
frame-box` — the page's registration frame (hairlines + corner marks), not a window.
copy-button` — the clipboard control the address bar composes; reach for it directly to copy any other value.
bestPractices: Compose the default slot exactly as the screen would be composed in an app — the frame mirrors the page's stylesheets and theme into its viewport, so no extra wiring or classes are needed.
Pin the device the example is about with `v-model:width` and `v-model:height` (`375 × 812` mobile, `768 × 1024` tablet, `1280 × 800` desktop); leave `width` unset to fill the container.
Give the frame an `ariaLabel` that names what is shown (`Pricing page at tablet size`); it becomes the viewport's accessible name.
Viewport-height units (`h-screen`, `min-h-dvh`) in slot content resolve against the simulated height, so a full-height shell renders as it would on the device.
Do not add controls to the chrome — the address's copy button and the resize handles are the frame's only controls. Interactive content belongs in the default slot.

slots.notes: The `Accordion.Item` children. Each sub-component's own `default` slot is documented in the Sub-components section.

accordion.purpose: A vertically stacked set of disclosure items: each item has a clickable header that expands or collapses its content panel. Use it to condense long content into scannable sections. Unlike `tabs` (mutually-exclusive panels shown in place), an accordion can keep one item open at a time (`type="single"`) or several at once (`type="multiple"`), and its content expands inline below each header.
useWhen: Long content splits into independent sections the reader scans by heading and opens on demand (settings groups, help topics, a details list).
The reader may want one section open at a time (`type="single"`) or to compare several side by side (`type="multiple"`).
Content should expand inline below its heading, pushing the rest of the page down.
avoidWhen: The panels are mutually exclusive views shown in the same place → use `tabs`.
It is the frequently-asked-questions band of a marketing page → use `faq-section` (or `faq` for the band without the page-section wiring).
It is hierarchical navigation with expandable rows → use `menu`.
related: tabs` — switches between panels in place; one panel visible, headers in a row.
faq` — the marketing FAQ band that composes `accordion` with a heading column and hairline register.
menu` — expanding rows for navigation, not for revealing content.
bestPractices: Give every `Accordion.Item` a unique `value`; the open state is keyed by it, and `default-value` / `v-model` refer to it.
Bind `v-model` to a string in `type="single"` and to an array in `type="multiple"`; set `collapsible` to `false` only when one item must always stay open.
Set the trigger's `level` to fit the page outline (default `3`) — each trigger is wrapped in a real heading.
Accordion.Content` applies no padding; pad the content you put inside it.
Set `size` and `arrow-position` on the root, not per item — they are provided to every item through context.

accordion-root.purpose: A vertically stacked set of disclosure items: each item has a clickable header that expands or collapses its content panel. Use it to condense long content into scannable sections. Unlike `tabs` (mutually-exclusive panels shown in place), an accordion can keep one item open at a time (`type="single"`) or several at once (`type="multiple"`), and its content expands inline below each header.
useWhen: Long content splits into independent sections the reader scans by heading and opens on demand (settings groups, help topics, a details list).
The reader may want one section open at a time (`type="single"`) or to compare several side by side (`type="multiple"`).
Content should expand inline below its heading, pushing the rest of the page down.
avoidWhen: The panels are mutually exclusive views shown in the same place → use `tabs`.
It is the frequently-asked-questions band of a marketing page → use `faq-section` (or `faq` for the band without the page-section wiring).
It is hierarchical navigation with expandable rows → use `menu`.
related: tabs` — switches between panels in place; one panel visible, headers in a row.
faq` — the marketing FAQ band that composes `accordion` with a heading column and hairline register.
menu` — expanding rows for navigation, not for revealing content.
bestPractices: Give every `Accordion.Item` a unique `value`; the open state is keyed by it, and `default-value` / `v-model` refer to it.
Bind `v-model` to a string in `type="single"` and to an array in `type="multiple"`; set `collapsible` to `false` only when one item must always stay open.
Set the trigger's `level` to fit the page outline (default `3`) — each trigger is wrapped in a real heading.
Accordion.Content` applies no padding; pad the content you put inside it.
Set `size` and `arrow-position` on the root, not per item — they are provided to every item through context.

header-action` content stays hidden until the header is hovered or focused, so keep it to secondary actions and never make it the only way to reach a control.
Set `:padded="false"` only when the content draws its own inset or needs flush dividers.
The footer renders only when the `footer` slot has content; don't pass an empty template to reserve space.

card-pricing.purpose: One tier of a pricing table: what it is called, what it costs, what that price includes, and the one action that moves the account onto it. The card owns the typographic hierarchy of a price — an overline plan name, the amount as the headline figure, and the billing caveat under it in muted body copy — so a row of tiers reads as a comparison rather than as three differently-typeset cards. `slotPosition` is the axis that decides which of the two compositions the card is. **`bottom`** is the compact tier: the name, a `medium` amount and the caveat stack at the top, the action follows, and the slot sits under it — a card sized by its own content, for a row of tiers a reader scans. **`middle`** is the full tier: the amount becomes the `large` headline figure, the caveat moves up to `body-md`, the slot grows to fill the card, and the action is pinned to the bottom edge so a row of `middle` cards has its buttons on one line whatever each tier's feature list holds. `kind` decides only whether the card draws its own surface (`contained`) or sits on the one behind it (`transparent`); it never changes the composition. The name, the amount and the caveat are **one column**, capped at `--container-xs` (348px) rather than at the card's full width: the caveat is a sentence about the price directly above it, so it wraps on the price's measure. The cap shipped as `--container-3xs` (256px) — two rungs down the ladder, and too narrow for the copy it holds. 256px sets `body-md` at roughly 33 characters, under the 45–75 a prose measure wants, and all three billing caveats on the sample pricing page (66, 69 and 84 characters) ran to three lines there. At 348px the measure is ~46 characters and the same three set in two, while the card's own content box at 1440 is 413px — so the caveat is still held to the price's column instead of the card's. The card carries **one** prose region — the pricing caveat, below the amount. It used to carry a second paragraph above the amount as well, and with `aligned` reserving a band for each, a row of tiers showed two two-line muted blocks around every price doing the same visual job. The Figma component (`3605:2260`) has a single prose region, `Pricing Details`, positioned below the amount, so that is the one the card keeps; a tier's positioning sentence belongs to whatever the consumer puts in the slot. `aligned` makes a ROW of cards read as one comparison. Every region is content-sized by default, which is right for a single card and wrong for three side by side — a tier with a two-line caveat and a tier with none put their feature lists on different lines, and the reader has to re-find the row in every column. It reserves **three** lines for the caveat, in `lh` so the reservation follows the type token rather than a hard-coded height. Three is the design's 64px band expressed in whole lines of the region's own token (`body-md` is a 22px line box, so `3lh` is 66px; `2lh` is 44px and twenty short) — it shipped as `2lh`, and the shortfall stayed invisible until a tier's caveat ran to three lines at the region's then-256px measure, overflowed the band, and pushed that column's feature list 22px below the other two. Opt-in, because reserving empty lines is wrong for a lone card; set it on every card in the row. A caveat past three lines still pushes the row down, like any overflow. The plan title is an **overline** (`.text-overline-md` on an `<h3>`): the token carries the display face, the uppercase transform and the widest tracking step, so the tier reads as a label on the card rather than as a title competing with the price beneath it. It stays an `<h3>` for the document outline — the tier is the section heading — while looking like an overline.
useWhen: One tier in a row of plans: plan name, price, billing caveat, one action and the tier's feature list.
A compact tier sized by its content (`slot-position="bottom"`), or a full tier whose action is pinned to the bottom so a row's buttons line up (`slot-position="middle"`).
A tier set on the surface behind it (`kind="transparent"`) inside a section that already draws the frame.
avoidWhen: You need the whole plans band of a pricing page, with the billing-period toggle and the framed row → use `pricing-plans`.
You need a feature-by-feature comparison across plans → use `compare-plans`.
You only need to show an amount, in a table cell or a summary → use `currency`.
The card holds general content rather than a price → use `card`.
related: currency` — typesets the amount inside the card; use it directly for prices outside a tier card.
pricing-plans` — the page section that lays out a row of plan cards with the billing toggle.
compare-plans` — the matrix that sits under the plan cards.
card` — generic bordered card with header, content and footer regions.
bestPractices: In a row of tiers, set `aligned` on every card so each caveat reserves the same band and the feature lists start on one line.
Keep `pricing-details` to the billing caveat. A tier's positioning sentence goes in the default slot with the feature list.
The card emits no events, and the built-in button has no handler. To act on the click, fill the `actions` slot with your own `Button`.
Hide the symbol or the period with `:show-prefix="false"` / `:show-suffix="false"` (for example on a custom-quote tier) instead of clearing `prefix` / `suffix`.
Mark at most one card in a row with `show-tag` and `tag-label`.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: The panel's parts — `HelpPanel.Header`, `HelpPanel.Section`, `HelpPanel.Tutorial`, `HelpPanel.Links` — in reading order. Not rendered while `loading`.

help-panel.purpose: The content of a help side region: a topic's title, a few sections of short guidance, and the "Learn more" links that leave for the documentation — or, in tutorial mode, an ordered list of tasks with the reader's progress through them. It is the thing that goes **inside** a side region, not the region itself: the consumer places it in a `Drawer` or in the page's side rail, and that host owns opening, closing and the close button. It owns no open state, so it has no `Trigger` / `Content` and no `data-state="open|closed"`. Its anatomy is the anatomy of a help page — `Header`, `Section`, `Links`, `Tutorial`, `Task` — composed by hand, so a topic can omit the links, carry one section or five, or be a tutorial with no prose at all.
useWhen: A Console screen needs contextual help beside the work: what this page is for, what a field means, where the docs are.
A guided, multi-task tutorial runs beside the real UI, and the reader needs to see which task they are on and how many are done.
The help content is loaded asynchronously and the region must reserve its space while it arrives (`loading`).
avoidWhen: A one-line hint attached to a single control → use `doc-tooltip` or the field's `helper-text`.
The region itself (overlay, slide-in, close button, focus trap) → use `drawer`; put `help-panel` inside it.
Ordered steps the reader navigates between, with the step's form filling the column beside it → use `stepper`.
Numbered instructions inside a documentation page, read all at once → use `doc-steps` + `doc-step`.
A page with nothing configured yet, which needs one call to action → use `empty-state`.
related: drawer` — the host that opens, closes and traps focus around a help panel shown as an overlay.
stepper` — the same dot language for steps the reader navigates; tutorial tasks are reported, not navigated.
link` — the standalone link each `HelpPanel.Links` row is composed from.
button` — the Start / Continue / Restart controls the consumer composes into a tutorial's `actions` slot.
skeleton` — what the panel renders in place of its content while `loading`.
doc-prose` — long-form documentation prose; a help section is a few short paragraphs, not an article.
bestPractices: One topic per panel. When the reader moves to another part of the page, swap the panel's content — do not stack two headers.
Keep each `Section` to a short paragraph or a short list. If the reader has to scroll a section, the content belongs in the docs and the panel should link to it.
Title sections with the question the reader is asking (`What is a workload?`), not with a noun (`Overview`).
Put links to the documentation in `HelpPanel.Links`, at the end, not inline in every section.
In tutorial mode, exactly one task is `current`. Mark a task `complete` only when the real UI confirms it, never on click.
Close affordances belong to the host. Do not put a close button in `HelpPanel.Header`; the `Drawer` or side rail already has one.

props.name: title
props.doc: Headline of the section, rendered as the section's `h2`.

props.name: description
props.doc: Supporting sentence under the headline; overridden by the default slot.

props.name: eyebrow
props.doc: Short uppercase overline rendered above the headline.

props.name: kind
props.doc: Layout of the header: `centered` stacks and centers the copy, `left` stacks it at the start edge, `horizontal` sets the headline and its description in two columns.

props.name: size
props.doc: Step of the headline on the heading scale: `small` for a subsection inside a band, `medium` for an ordinary section opener, `large` for a band whose headline is the statement.

props.name: framed
props.doc: Draw the header's own frame and padding. Turn it off when the header is composed inside a band that already owns both.

props.name: padding
props.doc: Vertical padding of the framed header: `medium` for a section opener, `small` for a header that sits tight over its band.

props.name: descriptionWidth
props.doc: Width of the description in the horizontal layout: `narrow` keeps it to the third column, `wide` runs it across the middle column too.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: Description body; replaces the `description` prop when provided.

slots.name: actions
slots.notes: Call-to-action row under the copy, aligned with the chosen `kind`.

section-title.purpose: The framed header row that opens a page section: an optional overline, the section's `h2`, an optional description and an optional row of actions, held inside a registration frame whose bottom rule is what divides the header from the section body. `kind` picks the layout — `centered` for a symmetric opener, `left` for a reading-order one, and `horizontal` for a wide row that sets the headline against its description.
useWhen: Opening a marketing or landing page section that needs a framed header.
Whenever the header itself should carry the rule that separates it from the content below, with no extra margin.
For a wide band whose headline and supporting sentence should sit side by side rather than stacked — `kind="horizontal"`.
avoidWhen: For the page's leading band and its `h1` → use `hero` instead.
For the top bar of an application shell → use `global-header` instead.
For a plain framed container with arbitrary content → use `frame-box` instead.
related: hero` — the opening band; its `Hero.Title` renders the page's `h1` at hero scale.
frame-box` — the frame this component composes.
section-gap` — the empty frame that sets the air before and after a section header; this component holds no vertical air of its own beyond its padding.
overline` — the eyebrow treatment rendered above the headline.
bestPractices: Leave `framed` on when the header is a brick of its own in a page column; turn it off when a band composes the header inside a frame it already draws, so the rule and the padding are not drawn twice.

Keep one `section-title` per section, and let it own the section's `h2` so the page keeps one document outline. `size` changes the headline's step on the type scale, never its heading level — a page with a `large` and a `small` header still reads as two `h2`s.

Leave `size` at `medium` for an ordinary section opener. Reach for `large` only where the headline is the band's whole statement, and for `small` where the header opens a subsection inside a band that already has one.
Write the eyebrow as one or two words: it is set uppercase and prefixed with `//`, so a sentence in it reads as noise.
Reach for `horizontal` when the description is long enough to earn its own column — on a narrow viewport it stacks back under the headline.

In `horizontal`, set `--section-title-headline-span` to `2` from the consumer's class to run the headline across the middle column too, when it would otherwise wrap to three lines; the description keeps the third column, and the default `1` leaves that column as air. `--section-title-headline-max` caps the headline's width inside its span (`none` by default), so a headline that would fit on one line across two columns still breaks into two.

In `horizontal`, set `descriptionWidth="wide"` when the description runs to a paragraph and would stack six or more lines in the third column alone; it then spans the middle and third columns, capped at `--container-xl` and aligned to the right edge so it ends where the narrow description ends. It takes the column a `--section-title-headline-span` of `2` would claim, so use one or the other. Outside `horizontal` the prop has no effect.
Put the section's CTAs in the `actions` slot rather than in the body; the slot already stacks them fluid below `sm` and aligns them with the chosen `kind` above it.
The vertical rhythm around the header belongs to the `section-gap` frames on either side, not to this component.

props.doc: Item root surface variant. `inline` removes the row's outer padding (transparent surface) for inline placement and divided in-card lists.

props.name: size
props.doc: Item root density (padding and gap).

props.name: asChild
props.doc: Merge row layout and interactive-state classes onto the single default-slot child (e.g. anchor).

slots.name: default
slots.notes: Every sub-component exposes `default` for its region.

item.purpose: Versatile flex row for title, description, media, and actions. Mirrors the shadcn-vue Item anatomy so consumers can reorder or omit regions. Compose with `ItemGroup` for gapped off-card lists, `ItemList` for divided in-card lists (inside a `Card`), and `ItemSeparator` between rows. Reference: https://www.shadcn-vue.com/docs/components/item (adapted to Webkit tokens and naming).
useWhen: A row that pairs a title and description with leading media (icon, avatar, image) and trailing actions — settings entries, team members, next steps, notifications.
A list of such rows: `Item.Group` for gapped rows off a card, `Item.List` for divided rows inside a `card`.
A whole row that is one link or button — set `as-child` and pass a single `a` / `button` as the item's child.
avoidWhen: Records that share columns and need sorting, selection or paging → use `table`.
Hierarchical navigation rows in a sidebar → use `menu`.
A grid of selectable option cards → use `radio-cards`.
A single surface that frames arbitrary content → use `card`.
related: card` — the surface an `Item.List` sits in (with `:padded="false"`).
table` — columnar data; below `sm`, `listing-table` swaps its table rows for `item` rows.
menu` — navigation rows with nesting and drill levels.
avatar` — the usual leading media for people rows inside `Item.Media`.
bestPractices: Use `Item.Group` off-card and `Item.List` inside a `card` with `:padded="false"`; both force their child items' `kind` (`inline` in a group, `default` in a list), so do not set `kind` on rows inside them.
Item.List` draws its own dividers — do not add `Item.Separator` inside it.
With `as-child`, pass exactly one child element; the row's hover, active and focus ring move onto it, so do not also put buttons inside that row.
Set `Item.Media` `kind="icon"` for a glyph and `kind="image"` for a picture; the frame sizes and clips the content.
Use `size="small"` for dense lists; `medium` is the default.

item-root.purpose: Versatile flex row for title, description, media, and actions. Mirrors the shadcn-vue Item anatomy so consumers can reorder or omit regions. Compose with `ItemGroup` for gapped off-card lists, `ItemList` for divided in-card lists (inside a `Card`), and `ItemSeparator` between rows. Reference: https://www.shadcn-vue.com/docs/components/item (adapted to Webkit tokens and naming).
useWhen: A row that pairs a title and description with leading media (icon, avatar, image) and trailing actions — settings entries, team members, next steps, notifications.
A list of such rows: `Item.Group` for gapped rows off a card, `Item.List` for divided rows inside a `card`.
A whole row that is one link or button — set `as-child` and pass a single `a` / `button` as the item's child.
avoidWhen: Records that share columns and need sorting, selection or paging → use `table`.
Hierarchical navigation rows in a sidebar → use `menu`.
A grid of selectable option cards → use `radio-cards`.
A single surface that frames arbitrary content → use `card`.
related: card` — the surface an `Item.List` sits in (with `:padded="false"`).
table` — columnar data; below `sm`, `listing-table` swaps its table rows for `item` rows.
menu` — navigation rows with nesting and drill levels.
avatar` — the usual leading media for people rows inside `Item.Media`.
bestPractices: Use `Item.Group` off-card and `Item.List` inside a `card` with `:padded="false"`; both force their child items' `kind` (`inline` in a group, `default` in a list), so do not set `kind` on rows inside them.
Item.List` draws its own dividers — do not add `Item.Separator` inside it.
With `as-child`, pass exactly one child element; the row's hover, active and focus ring move onto it, so do not also put buttons inside that row.
Set `Item.Media` `kind="icon"` for a glyph and `kind="image"` for a picture; the frame sizes and clips the content.
Use `size="small"` for dense lists; `medium` is the default.

props.doc: Size token; affects typography and the gap between the figure and the suffix.

currency.purpose: Typesets one monetary amount as three separately-styled parts — the currency symbol, the figure, and a trailing period or unit — so money reads the same everywhere in the product instead of being a formatted string each screen spells its own way. The suffix carries the code typeface (`text-label-code-*`), which keeps the unit visually subordinate to the figure and aligns the whole set with the way the system typesets metered values. The size ladder is the house one (`small` / `medium` / `large`) and each step is a different reading distance: `small` is an amount inside a table row or a list cell, `medium` an amount stated as a fact on a card, `large` the headline figure of a pricing card. `large` bottom-aligns the suffix against the figure rather than centring it, because a 56px numeral centred against a 14px unit reads as two unrelated pieces of text.
useWhen: Any monetary amount in the product: a price in a table row or list cell (`small`), an amount stated on a card (`medium`), the headline figure of a pricing card (`large`).
An amount followed by a period or unit (`/ mon`, `/ GB`) that should read as secondary to the figure.
avoidWhen: You need a full pricing tier with plan name, caveat and action → use `card-pricing`.
The headline figures are not money (throughput, uptime, points of presence) → use `big-numbers`.
related: card-pricing` — composes Currency for its price, `medium` or `large` depending on `slotPosition`.
big-numbers` — display-scale figures for metrics that aren't money.
stats-band` — page section of big figures with their own prefix and unit.
bestPractices: Pass `value` already formatted as a string (`'1,250.00'`). The component does no number or locale formatting.
prefix` defaults to `'$'`; set `prefix=""` to drop the symbol. The suffix renders only when `suffix` is set.
Pick `size` by reading distance, not by available space: `small` (the default) in tables and lists, `medium` on cards, `large` only for a headline price.
Don't restyle the parts with classes; each size takes its typography from the `text-amount-*` and `text-label-code-*` tokens.

props.name: name
props.doc: Name of an official scene in the illustration asset library.

props.name: ariaLabel
props.doc: Accessible name; empty keeps the illustration decorative and hidden from assistive tech.

illustration.purpose: Renders an **official product illustration** — one of the scenes drawn in the Assets library in Figma and exported as an SVG that ships with this package. `name` selects a scene from a closed registry; there is no way to assemble artwork out of markup, so a page can only render illustrations design has actually signed off, and a scene can never drift between the screens that use it. The library is drawn once, in dark mode. The scene is drawn into the page as inline SVG and every colour it carries is repainted from the `illustration` theme foundation of `@aziontech/theme` — `--illustration-*` roles that alias the global tokens — so the one export follows light and dark like the rest of the page.
useWhen: An empty state, error page, onboarding step, or marketing tile needs a diagrammatic illustration of a product concept (a deploy, a request path, a connected service).
The same concept appears on more than one screen and must be the same drawing every time.
The artwork must scale to its container without rasterizing or re-exporting.
avoidWhen: A single glyph is enough → use an icon from `@aziontech/icons` (`<i class="ai ai-…">`).
The artwork is a brand mark (a client logo, a framework mark) → those are brand assets, not illustrations.
The whole component is "no data here, with a title and an action" → use `empty-state`, which already owns that layout and may embed an `Illustration`.
The graphic is a live data visualization → that is a chart, not an illustration.
The scene you need is not in the registry → it has to be drawn in Figma and exported first. Do not approximate it in markup.
related: empty-state` — the surrounding layout (illustration + title + description + actions); reach for it first and put an `Illustration` inside it.
flow` — a real interactive node/edge diagram driven by data; `Illustration` is decorative and static by comparison.
skeleton` — the loading placeholder; an illustration is never a loading state.
svg/azion/*` — drawn brand marks, for artwork that is not part of the illustration library.
bestPractices: Leave the illustration decorative (no `ariaLabel`) unless it carries information the surrounding copy does not. A decorative illustration is hidden from assistive tech, which keeps screen readers out of a graphic that adds nothing.
Size the illustration from the call site with a class. The root is `w-full` at the canvas aspect ratio, so a narrower column simply gets a smaller scene.
Pick the scene that draws the claim next to it, not the one whose filename matches the page title.
To add a scene, export the frame from the Figma assets library at 592×300, drop the `.svg` into `src/assets/illustrations/`, and register it. Never hand-draw one.
Leave `<Illustration />` unnamed where a scene is still being drawn: the placeholder frame reserves the space and reads as unfinished on the screen, which is louder than a gap nobody notices.

props.doc: Tab a tabbed widget plays (`workload-overview`, `application-version`, `functions-start`); other widgets ignore it, and unset plays the first tab.

props.name: interval
props.doc: Milliseconds between revealed log lines in the deploy logs widget; unset keeps its own pace.

product-widget.purpose: Draws one of the **official console widgets**: a scaled, inert mock of an Azion Console screen or fragment, built from real webkit components inside a `shell-mockup` frame, that marketing bands use to show the product. `name` selects the widget from a closed registry of 70 drawings, loaded on demand, so a page can only render mocks that already exist and the same screen is the same drawing on every page that shows it. The remaining props pass through to the widget that declares them, and a widget that does not declare one keeps its own value.
useWhen: A product band (hero, media split, feature tab, widget grid cell) needs to show a console screen or a fragment of one.
The same console screen appears on more than one page and must be the same drawing on each.
Several widgets share one slot (tabs), and only the one showing should play: drive `active` from the host.
A grid cell plays its fragment's beat while the pointer is over it: drive `hover` from the host.
avoidWhen: The screen you need is not in the registry → compose it with `shell-mockup` and its parts, then add it to the registry. Do not approximate it at the call site.
A live, working screen at a device size → use `browser-frame`.
A static product concept drawing → use `illustration`.
A screenshot or clip in documentation → use `doc-frame`.
related: shell-mockup` — the frame every widget is drawn in; reach for it directly to compose a new screen.
illustration` — the same closed-registry pattern for static scenes.
texture-material` — the texture a full-screen widget grounds itself with through `texture`.
bestPractices: Give the host a size (a height or an aspect ratio). A widget fills its host and scales its design width to fit.

Host a framed widget (a full screen) in a wide panel, and a fragment in a grid cell with its own padding. Fragments are drawn bare and float on the cell's surface, so set `--mockup-fade-color` on the cell when it is not `--bg-canvas`.
Leave `kind`, `chrome`, `width`, `tab` and `interval` unset unless the host needs a different value: unset keeps the widget's own.
Keep the copy beside the widget saying what it shows. Every widget but `function-code` and the coding-agent switch of `functions-start` is hidden from assistive technology.

shell-mockup.purpose: A scaled, inert picture of an Azion Console screen, for marketing bands that show the product. The consumer composes the screen's body from real webkit components at a fixed design width; the frame draws the console shell around it (the slim console bar, the side rail with breadcrumbs and actions, or the previous console's top bar) and scales the whole drawing to fit its host. Each piece of the body is a `ShellMockup.Part` that travels in on its own beat once the mockup scrolls into view, so the screen assembles itself instead of appearing all at once.
useWhen: Showing a console screen or fragment on a marketing band: a hero, a media split, a feature tab, a widget grid cell.
Depicting a product workflow with real webkit controls instead of a screenshot, so the drawing follows the theme and stays sharp at any size.
Staggering the parts of a mock so they arrive in reading order when the band scrolls into view, and replaying that entrance each time a tab makes the mock active.
Drawing only a fragment of a screen (a list, a form row) floating on the band's own surface, with `kind="bare"` and `chrome` off.
avoidWhen: To show a real, working screen at a device size → use `browser-frame`; it renders live content in a true viewport, not a scaled picture.
For a static screenshot or clip in documentation → use `doc-frame`.
For an illustration scene → use `illustration`.
related: browser-frame` — a live, resizable viewport for real screens; `shell-mockup` is an inert, scaled drawing of the console.
texture-material` — the texture the frame grounds itself with when `texture` is set.
frame-box` — the page's registration frame a mockup band is often placed inside.
bestPractices: Compose the body at the design width (`width`, `mobileWidth`), not at the host's width; the frame scales the drawing, so sizes inside are design pixels.
Give the host a height (or an aspect ratio); the frame fills its host and derives its design height from it.
Number parts in reading order with `order`, starting at `0`; parts on the same beat land together.
Keep the mockup decorative: it is hidden from assistive technology unless `interactive` is set, so the band's own copy must say what the picture shows.
Set `active` from the host when several mockups share one slot (tabs), so only the visible one plays and it replays when it returns.
Tune a fade with the consumer-side custom properties `--mockup-fade-start` / `--mockup-fade-end` (or `--mockup-fade-edge` for `y`) and match its color to the host surface with `--mockup-fade-color`.

kbd.purpose: Kbd renders keyboard input — a single key or a shortcut combination — as a compact, non-interactive keycap. It reads like a real key: a bordered surface with a thicker bottom edge for depth. Modifier keys are passed as boolean props (`meta`, `shift`, `alt`, `ctrl`) and rendered with the correct OS-aware glyph (⌘ on macOS, Ctrl elsewhere), so consumers never hardcode platform symbols. Use it for shortcut hints in prose, menus, and control suffixes (e.g. the ⌘K hint in `command`).
useWhen: Show a keyboard shortcut or a single key inline (a ⌘K hint on a search button, an `Esc` hint in a dialog, `/` to focus search).
Present a modifier combination whose glyph should adapt to the user's OS.
avoidWhen: The token is a status/category label, not a key → use `tag` or `badge`.
You need an interactive control that fires on click → use `button` / `icon-button`; Kbd is a presentational hint only.
related: command` — consumes Kbd for its per-item shortcut hints and its ⌘K trigger affordance.
badge` — compact non-interactive indicator for counts/status; Kbd is specifically for keyboard keys.
bestPractices: Keep the default slot to a single key or glyph (`K`, `7`, `Enter`, `Esc`, `/`); avoid lowercase words or sentences.
Pass modifiers as boolean props rather than hardcoding `⌘`/`⇧` so the glyph adapts to the OS.
Place surrounding punctuation outside the element, not inside the keycap.

key-value-pairs.purpose: A grid of labelled facts about one subject: each pair is a key (the term) and its value, which may be plain text or a composed component such as a `Link`, `Tag`, `CopyButton` or `StatusIndicator`. It renders a native description list laid out in 1 to 4 responsive columns, optionally split into titled groups, and owns its loading and empty-value surfaces. It replaces the hand-rolled label/value grids the resource detail templates (`ResourceSummary`, the detail Overview tabs) draw today.
useWhen: The facts band of a resource detail or Overview page: ID, status, region, created at, domain.
A read-only summary of settings before a confirm step (review step, deploy summary).
Any set of named attributes of a single subject where the reader scans keys to find a value.
Facts that fall into named clusters (General, Networking, Source) shown side by side as titled columns.
avoidWhen: Rows of many subjects compared attribute by attribute → use `table`.
Editable fields → use the form field components (`field` with `input`, `select`, …); this component is read-only.
A single headline figure with a trend → use `stat-tile`.
A list of items with no key/value relation → use a plain list or `item`.
related: table` — many subjects, one row each; KeyValuePairs describes one subject.
card` — the surface a KeyValuePairs usually sits in; KeyValuePairs brings no surface of its own.
copy-button` — the trailing copy affordance for IDs and keys inside a value.
status-indicator`, `tag` — status and category values.
link` — a value that navigates (a domain, a linked resource).
hint` — the info glyph composed into an Item's `info` slot.
skeleton` — rendered in place of each value while the root is `loading`.
bestPractices: Keep keys short nouns in sentence case ("Created", "Region"), never sentences or trailing colons.
Order pairs by what the reader looks for first: identity, status, then the rest.
Use `columns` for width, not for grouping; use `KeyValuePairs.Group` when the facts form named clusters, one group per column.
Do not mix bare Items and Groups at the same level; pick one shape per instance.
Leave the value slot out (or render nothing in it) when a value is absent; the component shows the em dash and its accessible "Not set". Do not type your own "-", "N/A" or "None".
Put a `CopyButton` after an ID or key, never in place of the visible value.
Use the `info` slot for a short `Hint` that explains the key; long explanations belong in the page, not in a tooltip.
Drive `loading` from the data request so the labels stay in place and only the values shimmer.
