Any set of named attributes of a single subject where the reader scans keys to find a value.
Facts that fall into named clusters (General, Networking, Source) shown side by side as titled columns.
avoidWhen: Rows of many subjects compared attribute by attribute → use `table`.
Editable fields → use the form field components (`field` with `input`, `select`, …); this component is read-only.
A single headline figure with a trend → use `stat-tile`.
A list of items with no key/value relation → use a plain list or `item`.
related: table` — many subjects, one row each; KeyValuePairs describes one subject.
card` — the surface a KeyValuePairs usually sits in; KeyValuePairs brings no surface of its own.
copy-button` — the trailing copy affordance for IDs and keys inside a value.
status-indicator`, `tag` — status and category values.
link` — a value that navigates (a domain, a linked resource).
hint` — the info glyph composed into an Item's `info` slot.
skeleton` — rendered in place of each value while the root is `loading`.
bestPractices: Keep keys short nouns in sentence case ("Created", "Region"), never sentences or trailing colons.
Order pairs by what the reader looks for first: identity, status, then the rest.
Use `columns` for width, not for grouping; use `KeyValuePairs.Group` when the facts form named clusters, one group per column.
Do not mix bare Items and Groups at the same level; pick one shape per instance.
Leave the value slot out (or render nothing in it) when a value is absent; the component shows the em dash and its accessible "Not set". Do not type your own "-", "N/A" or "None".
Put a `CopyButton` after an ID or key, never in place of the visible value.
Use the `info` slot for a short `Hint` that explains the key; long explanations belong in the page, not in a tooltip.
Drive `loading` from the data request so the labels stay in place and only the values shimmer.

props.name: region
props.doc: Which part of the world has its PoPs lit; the map always frames the whole world.

props.name: density
props.doc: How many PoPs are lit, from `none` to `high`.

props.name: animated
props.doc: Pulses the PoPs in three staggered waves; static when false.

props.name: opacity
props.doc: Opacity of the landmass dots, from 0 to 1; the PoPs stay at full strength.

props.name: position
props.doc: Where the map parks in the space the box leaves over.

props.name: scale
props.doc: Size of the map relative to the box; 1 fits it, below 1 shrinks it toward its position, above 1 enlarges it.

props.name: offsetX
props.doc: Horizontal shift as a fraction of the map width; negative moves it left, positive right, past the box edge if large enough.

props.name: offsetY
props.doc: Vertical shift as a fraction of the map height; negative moves it up, positive down, past the box edge if large enough.

props.name: fade
props.doc: Fades the map out along an axis so it meets content without a hard edge.

network-map.purpose: A decorative, full-bleed layer that paints the dotted world map with Azion's PoPs lit in the brand accent. It is a material — it takes no content and claims no space — but unlike a static illustration it is tuned by the consumer (region, PoP density, landmass opacity, static or animated) to sit behind a band's copy.
useWhen: As the backdrop of a band whose subject is the network (reach, data centers, latency, resilience), composed as a sibling under the band's copy inside a positioned, clipping ancestor.
When a band is about one part of the network, so only that region's PoPs should light (`region`) while the whole world stays drawn.
When the same artwork has to read with more or fewer PoPs lit, or with none at all (`density="none"`), from one component instead of separate exports.
avoidWhen: For a real node/edge diagram driven by data → use `flow`.
As a wrapper around content. The layer is absolutely positioned and paints only itself; content is a sibling above it.
related: frame-box` — the ruled box a network band usually sits in; it supplies the positioned, clipping ancestor.
bestPractices: Give the layer a positioned ancestor (`relative overflow-hidden`); it fills that box and nothing else.

Never offset or resize the layer with utilities (`left-*`, `w-*`, `inset-*`). It always fills its positioned ancestor, and `position` + `fade` place the map inside that box — so a fade measures from the band's own edges. An offset box moves the fade's edges off the band's and makes the two placements fight.

To make the map smaller or larger inside its box, set `scale` instead of resizing the layer. The map shrinks toward its `position` corner, so there is no hard edge and the fade keeps measuring from the band's edges.
Keep `opacity` low (the default `0.4`) when copy sits over the landmass; the PoPs keep full strength so the network still reads.
For copy on one side of a band, park the map on the other side with `position` and fade it toward the copy (`position="right"` + `fade="left"`); the default stops need no consumer class.
Tune where a fade holds and ends with `--network-map-fade-start` / `--network-map-fade-end` only when the default stops do not fit, instead of adding masks.
Leave `animated` off by default; turn it on for the one band per page whose subject is the network.
To nudge the map or let it run off the band, set `offsetX` / `offsetY` (for example `:offset-x="0.15"` to bleed right, `:offset-y="-0.1"` to bleed up) instead of offsetting the layer.
asia` and `oceania` hold no PoPs — the artwork carries no accent field there — so either region lights none and the map reads as landmass alone.

examples.name: Default
examples.summary: The whole world at medium density. The layer fills its nearest positioned ancestor, so the box it sits in is what gives it a size; `position` parks the map in the room `scale` leaves, and `offsetX` / `offsetY` shift it from there, past the box edge when large enough.

examples.name: Regions
examples.summary: Every region, each lighting only its own PoPs over the same whole-world map. `asia` and `oceania` hold no PoPs, so they read as landmass alone.

examples.name: Densities
examples.summary: Levels are cumulative: `low` lights 65 PoPs, `medium` 186 and `high` 275. `none` draws the landmass alone.

log-view.purpose: Composition-based terminal log viewer for CI/deploy output. **LogView** is the root shell and context provider; **LogViewHeader**, **LogViewContent**, and **LogViewFooter** are composed as children so teams can reorder, omit, or replace the toolbar and footer without forking the log renderer.
useWhen: Showing build, deploy or CI output as timestamped lines the reader can search, filter to warnings, and copy.
A log shell whose toolbar and footer vary by screen — compose `LogViewHeader`, `LogViewContent` and `LogViewFooter` in the order you need, or drop the ones you don't.
A log that is still loading from the server — set `loading` to show a spinner and `loading-label` in place of the body.
avoidWhen: Static, read-only code or configuration snippets → use `code-block`.
An animated terminal session on a marketing page → use `cli-terminal`.
Rows of structured records with columns, sorting or paging → use `table`.
related: code-block` — highlighted source code with a copy action, not a stream of typed log lines.
cli-terminal` — marketing band that plays a scripted terminal session.
deploy-success` — the post-deploy screen that embeds `log-view` for the build log.
bestPractices: Give every line a stable `id` and a `type` (`text`, `folder`, `framework-version`, `success`, `warning`); the type drives the line's rendering and the warnings filter.
Bind `v-model:search` and `v-model:warnings-only` when the app needs the filter state; otherwise leave them unbound and the header manages them.
Set `:bordered="false"` when the log sits inside a surface that already frames it (an accordion panel, a drawer).
The copy control hides while `disabled` or `loading`, or when there is nothing to copy; listen to `@copy` for the copied text instead of reading the clipboard.
Use the header's `left` / `right` / `search` slots and the footer's default slot to add actions, rather than rebuilding the toolbar.

examples.name: Default
examples.summary: LogViewHeader + LogViewContent over a realistic deploy log. Search filters lines and highlights matches in the body.
examples.sfc:
<script setup>
  import LogView from '@aziontech/webkit/log-view'
  import LogViewHeader from '@aziontech/webkit/log-view-header'
  import LogViewContent from '@aziontech/webkit/log-view-content'
  import { ref } from 'vue'

  const lines = [
    { id: '1', time: '13:47:33', type: 'text', message: 'Deploy started successfully!' },
    { id: '2', time: '13:47:41', type: 'success', message: 'Build finished' },
    {
      id: '3',
      time: '13:47:42',
      type: 'folder',
      message: 'dist/index.js',
      folderType: 'asset',
      size: '12.4 kB',
      gzipSize: '4.1 kB'
    },
    { id: '4', time: '13:47:43', type: 'warning', message: 'Bundle larger than recommended' }
  ]
  const search = ref('')
  const warningsOnly = ref(false)
</script>

<template>
  <LogView
    :lines="lines"
    v-model:search="search"
    v-model:warnings-only="warningsOnly"
    class="h-[640px]"
  >
    <LogViewHeader />
    <LogViewContent />
  </LogView>
</template>

code-block.purpose: Read-only code viewer for docs, API examples, and configuration previews. Supports four Figma-documented layouts that share one monolithic shell: 1. **Language switcher** ([4567:33761](https://www.figma.com/design/t97pXRs7xME3SJDs5iZ5RF/Webkit?node-id=4567-33761)) — tabbed snippets with a sliding pill, optional filename bar, syntax highlighting, and copy. 2. **Show filename** ([4567:30198](https://www.figma.com/design/t97pXRs7xME3SJDs5iZ5RF/Webkit?node-id=4567-30198)) — single snippet with a raised filename bar (language icon + name), no tabs. 3. **Diff** ([4567:29012](https://www.figma.com/design/t97pXRs7xME3SJDs5iZ5RF/Webkit?node-id=4567-29012)) — per-line added/removed markers (`+`/`-`), semantic row backgrounds, and a 2 px leading bar; no tabs or filename bar. 4. **Highlighted line** ([4567:31473](https://www.figma.com/design/t97pXRs7xME3SJDs5iZ5RF/Webkit?node-id=4567-31473)) — one active line with info background and leading bar; no tabs or filename bar. Regions render conditionally from tab data — the consumer does not pick a separate `kind`. Tab header appears when `tabs.length > 1`. Filename bar appears when the active tab sets `fileName`. Diff and highlight decorations come from `lineChanges` and `highlightedLine` on the active tab. **Syntax highlighting** is driven by the active tab's `language` and resolves to one of these tokenisers, all of which emit the same seven token types (`keyword`, `string`, `function`, `type`, `punctuation`, `identifier`, `comment`) so every language shares the one `--code-sintax-*` palette:
useWhen: Read-only code in docs, API examples or configuration previews that readers copy from.
The same snippet in several languages, switched by tabs (one `tabs` entry per language).
Showing a change as a diff (`lineChanges`) or pointing at one line (`highlightedLine`) on the active tab.
avoidWhen: The content is build or deploy output with timestamps and log levels → use `log-view`.
It is a marketing band that pairs a claim with its code → use `code-split`, or `sticky-scroll-code` for several claims.
It is a terminal session of CLI commands on a product page → use `cli-terminal`.
You only need to copy one short value (a token, an ID) without showing a block → use `copy-button`.
related: copy-button` — the copy control CodeBlock embeds; use it alone for one-line values.
log-view` — terminal-style viewer for CI and deploy logs.
code-split` — page section built around one code sample.
scroll-area` — the scroll container the code region runs in.
bestPractices: Put the source on each tab's `code`. There is no top-level `code` prop, and a tab without a `value` or a `code` is dropped.
Set `language` on every tab. Only JavaScript/TypeScript, shell, HCL, GraphQL and Markdown are tokenised; anything else renders as flat text.
Use `default-value` for the initial tab, and `v-model` only when something outside the block must follow the selected tab.
Set `:copyable="false"` on decorative blocks, and `:bordered="false"` when the block sits inside a surface that already frames it.
Keep `animate-lines` for marketing layouts; leave it off in docs and console screens.

props.name: maxHeight
props.doc: Max height (CSS length). The viewport scrolls dynamically: horizontal scroll appears automatically when columns overflow the width; vertical scroll appears only when `maxHeight` is set smaller than the content (under the sticky header).

props.name: bordered
props.doc: Draw the outer card border around the table. Off by default (the table is typically framed by a surrounding surface); set `bordered` / `:bordered="…"` to draw the `var(--border-default)` outline. The internal row dividers are unaffected.

props.name: data
props.doc: Data-driven mode: row records.

props.name: columns
props.doc: Data-driven mode: column definitions (`{ id?, accessorKey?, header?, label?, enableSorting?, grow?, principal?, frozen?, width?, minWidth?, align?, kind?, resizable?, hideable?, orderable? }`; `width` (px) sets a fixed pixel column (also needed when a frozen column precedes another frozen column on the same edge, so sticky offsets can be summed); **`minWidth`** (px) sets a **floor** instead: the table measures the column's own content — its header, including the sort affordance, and every rendered body cell — and pins the column to the larger of the two, as **one** width applied to the header and every body cell (a per-cell `min-width` would let each row size to its own content and drift the header away from the body). It is for a column whose content is a chip or a short token: a fixed `width` there is a bet in both directions — too generous and it reserves space the rest of the row needs, too tight and the chip inside it truncates. The measured width tracks the **rendered page**, so a column can change width when paging or sorting brings longer content into view; `width` wins when both are set, and a user resize wins over both. a `grow` column without `width` keeps a shared fixed basis so the header and body stay aligned and the cell never wraps. A column with no `grow` defaults to weight `2` for the **principal** column and `1` for the rest, so the columns fill the available space proportionally. The principal column is the one flagged `principal: true`, or — when none is flagged — the first non-action column. A `kind: 'action'` column is automatically pinned to the trailing (right) edge — staying reachable while the rest scrolls horizontally — and is never resizable. **`resizable: true`** opts a column into a live mouse/touch drag-to-resize handle on its header (native pointer events; the `@tanstack/vue-table` exception covers sorting/pagination/selection/visibility, not sizing). On the first drag of any divider every flexible column freezes at its current rendered width; from then on dragging changes **only that column** and the table grows (horizontal scroll) — the others are untouched. The drag floor is the column's own content width (header label + visible body cells), so a column never shrinks past its content. Frozen and action columns ignore `resizable`. **`label`** overrides the `Table.ColumnSelector` label when `header` is not a string; **`hideable: false`** excludes the column from `Table.ColumnSelector` (e.g. the actions column); **`orderable: true`** opts the column into `columnOrder`. When non-empty, the table renders itself via TanStack.

table.purpose: Composition primitives for building accessible, pixel-perfect data tables, in two modes. **Composition mode** (default): compose the anatomy by hand (header / body / rows / cells) — the component owns markup, tokens, a11y, configurable column sizing (an emphasized first column), sortable headers, selectable rows, and a **freeze system** for sticky columns (e.g. an actions column) and a sticky header. **Data-driven mode**: pass `data` + `columns` and the table renders itself via the headless **`@tanstack/vue-table`** engine, still rendering through the same primitives (our markup/tokens/a11y, pixel-perfect to Figma). Pairs with the [`Pagination`](./pagination.md) component (rendered automatically in the footer when `paginated`). A top **toolbar band** (`title` / `toolbar` / `filters` slots) sits above the scroll viewport in both modes for a title, search / filter / export / column-selector actions, and removable filter chips; the `toolbar` and `filters` slots are scoped with the TanStack `table` instance (in data-driven mode) so the consumer can drive filtering, global search, and column visibility through the table's own methods. **Engine.** Data-driven mode is driven by **`@tanstack/vue-table`** (`useVueTable` + `getCoreRowModel` / `getSortedRowModel` / `getFilteredRowModel` / `getPaginationRowModel`), covering sorting, pagination, row selection, column visibility, and global filtering — client- and server-side (`manualSorting` / `manualPagination` / `manualFiltering`). It is a pure-logic library (no markup/styles/positioning/animation), granted narrowly to this single component per [`.claude/rules/dependencies.md`](../.claude/rules/dependencies.md) § Exceptions; rendering stays 100% in our primitives. State is exposed via v-model (`sorting`, `rowSelection`, `columnVisibility`, `globalFilter`, `pagination`, plus the structured `filters` model and the aggregate `state` snapshot below). `@tanstack/virtual` remains forbidden. **Toolbar & imperative API.** The toolbar band composes context-aware controls that drive the table through the injected context with no wiring: `Table.Filter` (a structured field/operator/value builder that commits removable/editable filter chips, with an escape slot to plug a custom builder such as the console's AQL), `Table.AppliedFilters` (the chips), `Table.ColumnSelector` (a column-visibility picker over the existing `columnVisibility` state), `Table.Export` (CSV download), and `Table.RefreshButton`. Structured filters are a first-class model (`v-model:filters`, an `AppliedFilter[]` distinct from the free-text `globalFilter`) mapped to the TanStack column filters client-side, or emitted for a server refetch under `manualFiltering`. A `loading` prop renders skeleton rows for dynamic (server-side) data. The root exposes a **curated imperative API** via `defineExpose` (`reload`, `clearFilters`, `exportCsv`, `getState`, `setState`) so controls or logic outside the table can drive it through a template ref, and a serializable `TableStateSnapshot` (`sorting` / `pagination` / `columnVisibility` / `columnOrder` / `globalFilter` / `filters`) is exposed via `v-model:state` + `getState()` / `setState()` + an `initialState` seed — the component stays router-agnostic, so the consuming app owns any URL / localStorage persistence. examples.name: Default
examples.summary: A standard data-driven table: pass `:data` and `:columns` and the engine renders sortable headers, status `Tag`s, per-row action menus, and pagination. The outer card border is drawn via the `border` prop — the table is borderless by default (it usually sits inside a surface that already frames it), so set `border` to draw the `var(--border-default)` outline; the internal row dividers are unaffected either way.

examples.name: Composition
examples.summary: The compound API: build the table by hand from `<Table.Header>` / `<Table.Row>` / `<Table.HeadCell>` / `<Table.Cell>`. The result is an ordinary table — the same as the data-driven API — but you control every cell. Reach for it when a cell needs custom content; otherwise prefer `:data` + `:columns`.

examples.name: WithCheckboxes
examples.summary: A leading selection column (`enable-row-selection`): each row gets a checkbox and the header gets a select-all box that reflects the all/none/indeterminate state. Selection is exposed via `v-model:row-selection`; changes log to the Actions panel.

props.name: maxHeight
props.doc: Max height (CSS length). The viewport scrolls dynamically: horizontal scroll appears automatically when columns overflow the width; vertical scroll appears only when `maxHeight` is set smaller than the content (under the sticky header).

props.name: bordered
props.doc: Draw the outer card border around the table. Off by default (the table is typically framed by a surrounding surface); set `bordered` / `:bordered="…"` to draw the `var(--border-default)` outline. The internal row dividers are unaffected.

props.name: data
props.doc: Data-driven mode: row records.

props.name: columns
props.doc: Data-driven mode: column definitions (`{ id?, accessorKey?, header?, label?, enableSorting?, grow?, principal?, frozen?, width?, minWidth?, align?, kind?, resizable?, hideable?, orderable? }`; `width` (px) sets a fixed pixel column (also needed when a frozen column precedes another frozen column on the same edge, so sticky offsets can be summed); **`minWidth`** (px) sets a **floor** instead: the table measures the column's own content — its header, including the sort affordance, and every rendered body cell — and pins the column to the larger of the two, as **one** width applied to the header and every body cell (a per-cell `min-width` would let each row size to its own content and drift the header away from the body). It is for a column whose content is a chip or a short token: a fixed `width` there is a bet in both directions — too generous and it reserves space the rest of the row needs, too tight and the chip inside it truncates. The measured width tracks the **rendered page**, so a column can change width when paging or sorting brings longer content into view; `width` wins when both are set, and a user resize wins over both. a `grow` column without `width` keeps a shared fixed basis so the header and body stay aligned and the cell never wraps. A column with no `grow` defaults to weight `2` for the **principal** column and `1` for the rest, so the columns fill the available space proportionally. The principal column is the one flagged `principal: true`, or — when none is flagged — the first non-action column. A `kind: 'action'` column is automatically pinned to the trailing (right) edge — staying reachable while the rest scrolls horizontally — and is never resizable. **`resizable: true`** opts a column into a live mouse/touch drag-to-resize handle on its header (native pointer events; the `@tanstack/vue-table` exception covers sorting/pagination/selection/visibility, not sizing). On the first drag of any divider every flexible column freezes at its current rendered width; from then on dragging changes **only that column** and the table grows (horizontal scroll) — the others are untouched. The drag floor is the column's own content width (header label + visible body cells), so a column never shrinks past its content. Frozen and action columns ignore `resizable`. **`label`** overrides the `Table.ColumnSelector` label when `header` is not a string; **`hideable: false`** excludes the column from `Table.ColumnSelector` (e.g. the actions column); **`orderable: true`** opts the column into `columnOrder`. When non-empty, the table renders itself via TanStack.

pagination.purpose: Pagination controls for tables and lists, pixel-perfect to Figma, in two modes. **Composition mode** (default): a three-region landmark — page-info text, navigation buttons (Previous / page numbers / overflow / Next), and a rows-per-page selector — wired by hand through slots, with the consumer owning the current page, total, and page-size state. **Data-driven mode**: pass `total` (and optionally `page` / `pageSize`) and the Pagination renders its own info text, Previous / windowed page numbers / overflow ellipsis / Next, and the rows-per-page selector, emitting `update:page` / `update:pageSize` so the consumer can bind state via `v-model`. This component owns markup, tokens, and a11y; the data engine is a small internal page-window calculation — **no external pagination library**. Pairs with the [`Table`](./table.md) component.
useWhen: A list or table outside `table`'s own footer needs page navigation and a rows-per-page selector.
You know the item count — pass `total` and bind `v-model:page` / `v-model:page-size`; the component renders the info text, the windowed page numbers and the selector.
The page strip needs custom content (a different info line, extra controls) — compose `Pagination.Info`, `Pagination.Button` and `Pagination.PageSize` through the slots.
avoidWhen: The rows live in a data-driven `table` → set `paginated` on the table; it renders this pagination in its footer and wires it for you.
It is the previous / next pair at the end of a documentation page → use `doc-pagination`.
The content loads more as the reader scrolls or clicks "Load more" → use a `button` at the end of the list.
related: table` — renders a wired pagination in its footer when `paginated` is set.
doc-pagination` — previous / next links between documentation pages, not numbered pages of a list.
bestPractices: Prefer data-driven mode (`total` set); in composition mode the root emits nothing and you own every button's `selected` / `disabled` state and every click.
page` is 1-based. Changing the page size through the selector emits `update:pageSize` and resets the page to `1`.
Keep `page-size-options` aligned with what your data source accepts; the default is `[10, 25, 50, 100]`.
Tune `sibling-count` (default `1`) instead of hiding buttons — it controls how many numbers sit on each side of the current page before the overflow ellipsis.
Set `aria-label` when a page carries more than one pagination, so each navigation landmark has a distinct name.

examples.name: Default
examples.summary: The compound composition form: the full pagination assembled by hand from the dot-notation sub-components — page-info text (`Pagination.Info`), Previous / numbers / overflow / Next (`Pagination.Button`), and a rows-per-page selector (`Pagination.PageSize`).
examples.sfc:
<script setup>
  import Pagination from '@aziontech/webkit/pagination'
</script>

<template>
  <Pagination>
    <template #info>
      <Pagination.Info>Showing 1 to 10 of 20 entries</Pagination.Info>
    </template>

    <Pagination.Button
      kind="previous"
      aria-label="Previous page"
      disabled
    />
    <Pagination.Button
      kind="number"
      selected
      >1</Pagination.Button
    >
    <Pagination.Button kind="number">2</Pagination.Button>
    <Pagination.Button kind="number">3</Pagination.Button>
    <Pagination.Button kind="more" />
    <Pagination.Button
      kind="next"
      aria-label="Next page"
    />

    <template #controls>
      <Pagination.PageSize
        :model-value="10"
        :options="[10, 25, 50, 100]"
      />
    </template>
  </Pagination>
</template>

examples.name: Buttons
examples.summary: `Pagination.Button` kinds (previous / next / number / more) and states: default, selected (current page), and disabled. The buttons are butted into one segmented strip — the frame, border and end radii come from the `Pagination` root, so a consumer composes the buttons and nothing else.

examples.name: DataDriven
examples.summary: Data-driven mode: pass `total` and bind `v-model:page` / `v-model:page-size`. The Pagination renders its own info text, windowed page numbers, overflow ellipsis, and the rows-per-page selector, emitting `update:page` / `update:pageSize`.
examples.sfc:
<script setup>
  import Pagination from '@aziontech/webkit/pagination'
  import { ref } from 'vue'

  const page = ref(1)
  const pageSize = ref(10)
</script>

<template>
  <Pagination
    v-model:page="page"
    v-model:page-size="pageSize"
    :total="200"
    :page-size-options="[10, 25, 50, 100]"
    :sibling-count="1"
  />
</template>

bestPractices: Prefer data-driven mode (`total` set); in composition mode the root emits nothing and you own every button's `selected` / `disabled` state and every click.
page` is 1-based. Changing the page size through the selector emits `update:pageSize` and resets the page to `1`.
Keep `page-size-options` aligned with what your data source accepts; the default is `[10, 25, 50, 100]`.
Tune `sibling-count` (default `1`) instead of hiding buttons — it controls how many numbers sit on each side of the current page before the overflow ellipsis.
Set `aria-label` when a page carries more than one pagination, so each navigation landmark has a distinct name.

props.name: kind
props.doc: Button role within the pagination.

props.name: selected
props.doc: Marks the current page (filled surface + aria-current).

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Disables interaction and applies disabled tokens.

events.name: click
events.notes: Fires on activation. Not emitted while `disabled` (the native `disabled` attribute also blocks it), and never for `kind="more"`.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: The page number. Rendered only when `kind` is `number`.

pagination-button.purpose: PaginationButton is one segment of the pagination's numbers strip: a 28px-tall native `button` that renders a page number or a Previous / Next chevron, or — for `kind="more"` — an inert, decorative overflow ellipsis (`span`, `aria-hidden`), selected by `kind`. It is the part `pagination` renders in data-driven mode and the one consumers compose by hand in composition mode, where it is reached as `Pagination.Button` (or imported standalone from `@aziontech/webkit/pagination-button`). It owns the segment's surface, current-page (`selected`) and `disabled` treatment, but not the strip's frame, border or the page state, which belong to the `pagination` root and the consumer.
useWhen: Compose a custom page strip inside `pagination`'s default slot (composition mode), one button per Previous, page number, overflow and Next.
Render the current page of a hand-wired pagination with `selected`, and the unavailable Previous / Next ends with `disabled`.
avoidWhen: You know the item count → pass `total` to `pagination` and bind `v-model:page`; it renders and wires every PaginationButton itself.
The rows live in a data-driven `table` → set `paginated` on the table instead.
The control is a previous / next link between documentation pages → use `doc-pagination`.
It is a standalone action outside a pagination strip → use `button` or `icon-button`; this button has no radius or frame of its own except at the strip's ends.
It is a "Load more" control at the end of a list → use `button`.
related: pagination` — the root that frames the strip and, in data-driven mode, renders these buttons; re-exports this component as `Pagination.Button`.
pagination-info` — the page-info text that sits beside the strip.
pagination-page-size` — the rows-per-page selector placed in the pagination's `controls` slot.
icon-button` — a standalone icon-only action with its own frame and radius.
bestPractices: Place it only inside `pagination`'s default slot: the strip's border and frame come from the root, and the outer radius is applied through `first:` / `last:`, so only the first and last buttons of the strip round their corners.

Pass `aria-label` on every `previous` and `next` button: those kinds render an `aria-hidden` icon only and have no accessible name otherwise. `more` is decorative and hidden from assistive tech, so it takes no `aria-label`.
Put the page number in the default slot of `kind="number"` only; the other kinds ignore the slot.
Set `selected` on exactly one number button (it sets `aria-current="page"`), and `disabled` on Previous at the first page and Next at the last.
In composition mode you own every click: listen to `click` and update the page yourself; a `disabled` button never emits it.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: Diagram content: `flow-node` and `flow-parallel`, in flow order.

flow.purpose: Flow renders a directed flow diagram: a horizontal sequence of steps (`flow-node`) joined by decorative connectors, with optional parallel branches (`flow-parallel`) and custom connector-attachment points (`flow-anchor`). Use it to visualize pipelines, workflows, and step-by-step processes inside a data view; unlike `table` it expresses ordered/branching relationships rather than tabular records. Steps are written as direct children of `flow`; a `flow-parallel` between two steps fans out from the previous step and fans back into the next, and a `flow-parallel` at the start/end fans only inward/outward (no dangling stubs). A node can be styled (the default box) or `unstyled` so its slot content defines the entire node — a dot, a tall card, a multi-row card — while connectors still attach correctly, optionally at `flow-anchor` points inside the node. Connectors run port-to-port: a styled node renders a small square **connector port** just outside each of its edges, and a `flow-anchor` renders one outside the edge it attaches to, so a line always terminates on a visible attachment point instead of a bare edge (the port is the endpoint treatment — connectors carry no arrowheads). The port sits fully clear of the box rather than overlapping it, so neither the node's surface nor its focus ring crops it. A port is only rendered where a connector actually attaches: the leading child has no incoming connector and the trailing child no outgoing one, so those two edges show no port and the chain opens and closes on a node rather than on a stub. An `unstyled` node renders no ports, because its slot content owns its appearance; put a `flow-anchor` inside it to place ports on the parts a connector should touch. Design source (rewritten to our conventions, never inherited as-is): the kumo "Flow" component group at https://kumo-ui.com/components/flow/. Scope boundary: large diagrams pan via a native `overflow: auto` scroll container on the root — free 2D drag-pan is intentionally out of scope (it would require an external positioning library forbidden by `.claude/rules/dependencies.md`). The connector port is specified by the Figma frame in the frontmatter; the remaining tokens are inferred from intent and recorded in the Theme gaps table.
useWhen: Showing an ordered pipeline or request path as steps joined by connectors — build → deploy → serve, or a request through a load balancer, a function and its bindings.
A step fans out to several parallel targets and (optionally) back in — wrap those steps in `Flow.Parallel`.
A node with custom content (a card with several rows) where connectors must touch specific parts — mark them with `Flow.Anchor`.
avoidWhen: One of the official architecture drawings, or a node-and-connector picture for a marketing page → use `diagram`.
Tabular records with no ordering between them → use `table`.
A numbered set of instructions in documentation → use `doc-steps`.
related: diagram` — marketing architecture drawings from a closed library or a one-off spec; `flow` is the in-product, hand-composed pipeline.
doc-steps` — an ordered walkthrough of text steps joined by a rail, not connected nodes.
table` — records without ordered or branching relationships.
bestPractices: Write steps as direct children of `Flow` in flow order; connectors are drawn between siblings, so wrapping nodes in extra elements breaks the chain.

Use `unstyled` when the slot content is the whole node, and put a `Flow.Anchor` (`type="end"` incoming, `type="start"` outgoing) on each part a connector should touch — an unstyled node renders no ports of its own.
Mark a leaf that hangs off the chain with `terminal`; it receives a connector but sends none on.
Do not clip a node with `overflow-hidden` in a wrapping card — the connector ports sit outside the node's box and would disappear.
Let a wide flow scroll in its own container; the root is an `overflow: auto` region, and there is no drag-to-pan.

props.name: modelValue
props.doc: Bound pair of lists as `[sourceItems, targetItems]` (v-model).

props.name: dataKey
props.doc: Item field used as each row's render key (falls back to the index). Selection is always tracked by index.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Disables all selection and move controls and applies disabled tokens.

props.name: moveOnDoubleClick
props.doc: When true, double-clicking an item moves it to the opposite list. Set false to keep `item-double-click` firing without the move.

events.name: update:modelValue
events.notes: v-model update with the new `[sourceItems, targetItems]` pair.

events.name: move
events.notes: Fired after items move between lists, with the moved items.

events.name: item-double-click
events.payload: (event: MouseEvent, payload: { list: 'source' | 'target'; item: unknown; index: number })
events.notes: Fired when an option is double-clicked. `event` is the dblclick; `payload` carries the item, its index, and which list it was in. Fires regardless of `moveOnDoubleClick`, but not while the component is disabled or a list is loading.

slots.name: default
slots.scope: { move, moveAll, hasSelection, count, disabled, loading }
slots.notes: Composition slot; receives `<PickList.Source>`, `<PickList.Controls>`, and `<PickList.Target>` in flow order. The scope exposes the move actions plus selection/loading state, so a consumer can render custom controls inside the root in place of `<PickList.Controls>`.

pick-list.purpose: Dual-list transfer control: a labelled **source** listbox and a labelled **target** listbox with a control column to move items between them. Use it when the consumer needs to build a subset from a pool of options where both the chosen set and the remaining pool stay visible. Derived from the PrimeVue PickList behavior but rewritten to our conventions (no Figma); the visual surface is a best-effort first draft to validate. Compound, composition API: the root (`<PickList>`) owns the bound data (`v-model` = `[sourceItems, targetItems]`) and the shared selection/move state, and provides it through `provide`/`inject`. The consumer composes the anatomy — `<PickList.Source>`, `<PickList.Controls>`, `<PickList.Target>` — and the context-aware `<PickList.Controls>` wires the move buttons with no props. Each list is data-driven: items come from the root's bound pair and render through the list's `#item` slot (repeated data stays as props, not hand-authored rows). Double-clicking an option moves it to the opposite list (emitting `item-double-click`); this auto-move can be turned off with `move-on-double-click`. The two lists sit side by side on wider viewports and stack vertically (with the controls as a horizontal row between them) on narrow ones; the move arrows point left/right side-by-side and up/down when stacked.
useWhen: Building a subset from a pool where both the chosen and the remaining items stay visible (domains assigned to an application, members of a team).
Moving many items at once with move-all and multi-selection.
Lists that load separately, each with its own `loading` state.
avoidWhen: Picking a few values in a compact field → use `multi-select`.
Selecting rows of tabular data with columns, sorting, or pagination → use `table` with row selection.
A handful of fixed options → use a horizontal `field` with a `checkbox` for each.
related: multi-select` — compact dropdown for multi-pick when the remaining pool does not need to stay visible.
table` — row selection over tabular data.
checkbox` — independent boolean or small-set multi-pick.
bestPractices: Set `data-key` to a unique item field so rows keep stable keys across moves; without it rows are keyed by their index.
Set `title` on both `PickList.Source` and `PickList.Target`; it is the listbox's accessible name.
Listen to `move` for side effects such as saving the assignment instead of diffing `v-model`.
Set `:move-on-double-click="false"` when double-click should do something else; `item-double-click` still fires.

examples.name: Default
examples.summary: Two lists with select-and-move and move-all controls. Double-clicking an item moves it to the opposite list (and fires `item-double-click`); toggle the `moveOnDoubleClick` control to cancel the auto-move.
examples.sfc:
<script setup>
  import PickList from '@aziontech/webkit/pick-list'
  import { ref } from 'vue'

  const model = ref([
    [
      { id: 1, label: 'Edge Functions' },
      { id: 2, label: 'WAF' },
      { id: 3, label: 'Image Processor' }
    ],
    [{ id: 4, label: 'Cache' }]
  ])
</script>

<template>
  <PickList
    v-model="model"
    data-key="id"
  >
    <PickList.Source title="Available">
      <template #item="{ item }">{{ item.label }}</template>
    </PickList.Source>

    <PickList.Controls />

    <PickList.Target title="Selected">
      <template #item="{ item }">{{ item.label }}</template>
    </PickList.Target>
  </PickList>
</template>

props.name: items
props.doc: Nodes to render; each is `{ id: string; label: string; icon?: string; description?: string; disabled?: boolean; children?: TreeItem[] }`. A node with a non-empty `children` array is a parent.

props.name: selectable
props.doc: Enables single selection: activating a node writes its id to `v-model:selected` and marks it `aria-selected`.

props.name: loading
props.doc: Renders Skeleton rows in place of the tree and sets `aria-busy`.

props.name: emptyTitle
props.doc: Title of the default empty state shown when `items` is empty. Empty uses the locale catalog (`No items`).

props.name: emptyDescription
props.doc: Supporting line under the empty title.

props.name: ariaLabel
props.doc: Accessible name of the tree.

events.name: item-click
events.notes: A node activated: click on its row, or Enter / Space on the focused node. `item` is the consumer's own node object. Fires after `update:selected` when `selectable`. Not fired for a `disabled` node, nor for a click on the chevron or inside the `actions` region.

slots.name: item
slots.scope: { item: TreeItem; level: number; expanded: boolean }
slots.notes: Replaces the label region of every row (glyph + label + description). The fallback inside the slot renders `item.icon`, `item.label` and `item.description`. `level` is 1 for top-level nodes; `expanded` is false for leaves. The chevron, indentation, row states and the `actions` region stay owned by the tree.

slots.name: actions
slots.notes: Trailing per-row controls, end-aligned in the row (e.g. an `IconButton` that opens a `dropdown`). Clicks and keys inside it do not activate the row nor move tree focus. No fallback; when unused, the region is not rendered.

slots.name: empty
slots.notes: Replaces the default empty state. The fallback inside the slot is `EmptyState` titled by `emptyTitle` with `emptyDescription`.

tree.purpose: A hierarchical list of nodes, each row a name with an optional glyph and one line of detail, where a parent row folds its children open and closed under a chevron. It renders a nested `items` data structure on its own (recursively, through one internal row template) and follows the WAI-ARIA tree pattern, so it fits file and object browsers: the objects of a bucket, the source files of a deployment, the routes of an application. Unlike `menu` it navigates data, not the app, and unlike `accordion` its nodes are rows of the same kind at any depth, not panels of free content.
useWhen: Browsing a hierarchy whose depth is not fixed: bucket objects under folders, the source tree of a deployment, functions grouped by application.
Picking one node out of a hierarchy (`selectable`) to show its detail beside the tree.
A hierarchy the user expands piece by piece, where showing every level at once would bury the node they are after.
avoidWhen: Navigation between views of the app → use `menu` inside `sidebar`.
Flat records with several attributes each → use `table`.
A few sections of free content that open and close → use `accordion`.
A two- or three-level directory of destinations on a marketing page → use `column-navigation`.
related: table` — the flat, multi-column view of the same records; switch to it when columns matter more than nesting.
menu` — the hierarchical list for app navigation, with routes and active state instead of selection.
accordion` — disclosure of free content panels rather than rows of one kind.
empty-state` — what the tree renders when `items` is empty.
skeleton` — the rows the tree renders while `loading`.
bestPractices: Give every node an `id` that is unique across the whole tree, not only among its siblings; `v-model:expanded`, `v-model:selected` and focus are keyed by it.
Seed `v-model:expanded` with the path to the node the user is most likely after (the open folder, the selected file), not with every parent.
Keep labels short and put secondary detail (size, count, modified date) in `description` so rows scan as names first.
Use `selectable` only when the selection drives something on the screen (a detail pane, a preview); for a tree whose rows only lead somewhere, listen to `item-click` instead.
Put per-row controls in the `actions` slot (an `IconButton` that opens a `dropdown`), never inside the `item` slot, so they do not take over the row's activation.

examples.name: Default
examples.summary: A bucket-like file tree three levels deep, with glyphs and size descriptions. Two folders are seeded in `v-model:expanded`; the chevron and ArrowRight / ArrowLeft fold the rest.

examples.name: Selectable
examples.summary: With `selectable`, activating a node writes its id to `v-model:selected`, marks the row selected and sets `aria-selected`. The bound id is shown under the tree.

examples.name: CustomItem
examples.summary: The `item` slot replaces the label region of every row, here adding a status `Tag`; the `actions` slot adds an end-aligned `IconButton` per row. The chevron, indentation and row states stay owned by the tree.

props.name: kind
props.doc: Which admonition this is; drives the severity color and the icon.

props.name: label
props.doc: Fallback copy when the default slot is empty.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: The callout copy: prose with links and inline code, or paragraphs and a list, laid out by the callout since `DocProse` stops at its edge. The copy region is a flow container, so server-rendered block markup stays inside the box.

doc-callout.purpose: The admonition a documentation page interrupts itself with — Note, Info, Tip, Check, Warning, Danger — rendered on the webkit `Alert` surface, so the severity colour, the border, the icon and the radius come from the design system rather than from this layer. Its anatomy is a glyph and a column of prose — a sentence, or a few short paragraphs and a list — nothing else: no title row.
useWhen: An aside the reader must not miss mid-prose: a caveat, a prerequisite, a warning about data loss.
A short confirmation that a step worked (`check`), or a shortcut worth knowing (`tip`).
avoidWhen: For a block that needs its own box — a fenced sample, a table, a card grid. Those belong outside the callout; its body is prose, at most a short list.
For an application-screen banner or a form error — use `Alert` directly, which is what this composes.
As a section heading. A callout is an interruption, not structure.
related: Alert` — the webkit surface this renders on; reach for it directly outside documentation prose.
DocProse` — the contract around it. A callout marks itself `data-doc-chrome`, so prose rules stop at its edge, and `data-doc-block`, so it takes the block rung of the ladder.
bestPractices: Let the glyph and the tint carry the severity; do not restate it in the copy ("Warning: …").
Keep the body short — a sentence or two, links and inline code. A list is fine when the aside enumerates actions; the callout lays it out itself, because `DocProse` stops at its edge.
Reach for `tip` when the aside claims nothing about stakes. Borrowing `check` for a friendly shortcut paints a shortcut the same green as a confirmed success.

slots.name: icon

doc-card.purpose: One cell of the grid a documentation page scans across: a leading glyph, an optional eyebrow, the title, the copy, and an optional call-to-action row at the foot. It renders as an anchor when it has an `href` and as a plain block when it does not, so a card is either a destination or a statement — never a dead link.
useWhen: A grid of peer destinations: "what you can build", the product tiles a landing section opens with.
A set of short, scannable entries whose titles carry most of the meaning.
avoidWhen: When each entry needs a sentence to be understood — use `DocItem` rows, one column, so every description is read at the page's own measure instead of squeezed into a cell.
For a single call to action at the end of a page — that is a button, not a card.
For an application surface — use `Card`, which is the console's carded surface.
related: DocCardGroup` — the frame and grid this is a cell of; a card outside one has no cell ring.
DocItem` — the row counterpart. A card claims a whole tile; a row claims one line.
bestPractices: Keep the title to a noun phrase and let the copy carry the verb.
Use `eyebrow` only when the title alone does not say who or when; it is not a category label.
Set `link-label` when the card should close on an explicit call to action; otherwise the whole tile being the link is enough.

props.name: mobileColumns
props.doc: Column count on a phone. Two only pays when the cells are a mark plus a word.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: The `DocCard` children.

doc-card-group.purpose: The framed, responsive grid a `DocCard` set sits in. The group is the frame, not each card: `FrameBox` draws the perimeter and the four corner registration marks once around the whole set, the grid keeps 1px gaps, and every cell paints a 1px ring into them — so two neighbours share one hairline, an incomplete last row stays simply empty, and the set reads as one object the reader scans across rather than as loose tiles. `cols` names the widest column count; the grid always steps down toward one column on a phone unless a set of tiny cells opts into two with `mobileColumns`.
useWhen: Around every `DocCard` set — a card outside a group has no frame and no cell ring.
The fan-out at the top of a landing or section-index page: product tiles, a framework grid, a "what you can build" band.
avoidWhen: When each entry needs a full-measure sentence to be understood — use `DocItem` rows, one column, instead of cells.
As a general-purpose layout grid for application screens; it is documentation chrome, tied to the `DocProse` ladder.
related: DocCard` — the cell this frames; the group draws the perimeter and the cells paint the internal rules.
FrameBox` — the layout primitive that draws the frame and the corner registration marks.
DocProse` — the contract around it; `data-doc-block` puts the group on the block rung of the prose ladder.
bestPractices: Pick `cols` for the widest screen and let the breakpoints do the rest; do not wrap the group in another grid.
Leave `mobileColumns` at 1 unless every cell is a mark plus one word — a card with copy needs the whole phone width.
Let an incomplete last row be empty; do not stretch the last card to fill it.

props.name: caption
props.doc: Caption under the frame, centered; plain-text fallback for the caption slot.

props.name: hint
props.doc: Lead-in above the frame, left aligned; plain-text fallback for the hint slot.

props.name: src
props.doc: Media source; omit to frame slot content instead.

props.name: alt
props.doc: Alternative text for the framed media.

props.name: autoplay
props.doc: Plays the clip on its own, muted, inline and looping, with no controls.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: Framed content when no `src` is given.

slots.name: caption
slots.notes: Rich caption content; the `caption` prop is its plain-text fallback inside the slot.

slots.name: hint
slots.notes: Rich lead-in content; the `hint` prop is its plain-text fallback inside the slot.

doc-frame.purpose: The bordered surface every screenshot, diagram and clip in a documentation page sits on, so no media floats loose on the canvas and all of it shares one border, radius and inset. Pass `src` and the frame decides from the extension whether it holds a still or a clip; compose the default slot when the framed thing is markup. A still opens full screen out of its own frame — the picture is the button — while a clip keeps its player controls and composed content has no source to open. The caption reads under the frame, centered, as part of the picture; the hint reads above it on the text's own left edge, as part of the sentence that led the reader here; each is a string prop for the plain case with a slot of the same name for rich content.
useWhen: Any screenshot, diagram or screen recording inside documentation prose — every one of them, so the page's media all shares one border, radius and inset.
A composed panel or mock the page wants presented as a figure rather than as live UI: fill the default slot.
A clip that decorates a step (`autoplay`) or one the reader chooses to play (default, with controls).
avoidWhen: For an application-screen media block outside documentation prose — use `FrameBox` or compose the layout directly.
For an image that is itself a link or a card — a frame is a figure, not a navigation target.
For a gallery or carousel; the frame holds one piece of media at a time.
related: DocProse` — the page contract around it. The frame marks itself `data-doc-block`, so it takes the block rung of the prose ladder, and its caption and hint arrive unclassed for the page to style.
DocCallout` — the other block-level interruption; a callout carries words, a frame carries media.
bestPractices: Always pass `alt` for a still or a clip: it labels the media, names the zoom trigger, and titles the full-screen dialog.
Keep the caption to one line that belongs to the picture; a paragraph of context belongs in the prose above, or in `hint` when it leads directly into the frame.
Use the `caption` / `hint` slots only when the sentence needs markup (a link, a bold run, a code chip); the string props cover the plain case in one attribute.
Reach for `autoplay` only when the clip is decoration: it mutes, inlines and loops the clip and removes its controls, on the prop path and for a clip written by hand in the slot alike.

examples.name: Default
examples.summary: A frame around composed markup, with a caption under it. The default slot is what an author reaches for when the thing being framed is not a file.

examples.name: Media
examples.summary: One `src` covers both: a still renders as an image with its `alt`, and a source ending in a clip extension (`.mp4`, `.webm`, `.mov`, …) renders as a player, labelled from the same `alt`. A clip the reader chooses to play ships controls.

examples.name: Autoplay
examples.summary: A clip that plays on its own is decoration, so it must not seize the reader's speakers or take over an iOS viewport, and — with nobody there to replay it — it loops. `autoplay` therefore implies muted, inline and looping, and drops the controls. The frame applies the rule on both authoring paths: to the `autoplay` prop, and to a clip written by hand in the slot.

props.name: title
props.doc: The row's name — what the reader is choosing.

props.name: icon
props.doc: PrimeIcons class for the leading glyph.

props.name: href

props.name: target
props.doc: Where the link opens.

props.name: label
props.doc: Fallback copy when the default slot is empty.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: The row's copy: one or two sentences of inline prose.

doc-item.purpose: One row of the documentation's related-content list: a leading glyph in a framed 32px tile, the row's name, and the sentence that says what the thing is. When it has an `href` the title becomes an anchor stretched over the whole row — one tab stop, the full row as the hit area — closed by a trailing chevron, or a diagonal arrow when the destination leaves the documentation. The shell keeps `role="listitem"`, so a set of rows inside an `ItemList` is a real list to assistive technology.
useWhen: The "Related products" band a page ends on — peer destinations where each entry needs a sentence to be understood.
A one-column list of concepts or next steps, read at the page's own measure, with or without links.
avoidWhen: For a grid of scannable entries whose titles carry most of the meaning — use `DocCard` inside a `DocCardGroup`; a card claims a tile, a row claims one line.
For an application resource list — compose `Item` and its parts directly; this row is documentation chrome.
For a single call to action at the end of a page — that is a button, not a row.
related: DocCard` — the cell counterpart. A card claims a whole tile; this claims one line.
Item` / `ItemMedia` / `ItemContent` / `ItemTitle` / `ItemDescription` / `ItemActions` — the webkit anatomy this row composes.

FrameBox` + `ItemList` — the documented group pattern: the page draws one framed surface holding an `ItemList`, and the list rules between the rows. There is no `DocItemGroup` in the package; the group is this composition.
bestPractices: Keep the title to a noun phrase and let the sentence carry the verb; inline code in the sentence renders as the chip.
Give every row of one list the same shape — all with glyphs or none, all linked or none — so the column reads as one object.

Compose rows inside a `FrameBox` (with a solid surface) holding an `ItemList`: the frame draws the single box and the list draws full-width dividers, and the `role="list"` parent is what makes each row's `role="listitem"` valid.

examples.name: Default
examples.summary: Three linked rows in the documented composition — a `FrameBox` holding an `ItemList`. The link wraps the name and stretches over the row, so the whole row is the hit area with one tab stop per entry, and the trailing chevron says it travels.

props.name: items
props.doc: The headings, in document order.

props.name: activeId
props.doc: The id of the heading currently in view.

props.name: title
props.doc: The rail's own heading. Empty uses the locale catalog (`On this page`).

props.name: groups
props.doc: Complementary groups rendered below the outline, in order.

events.name: select
events.notes: Fired when a rail entry is activated; the page decides what scrolling means. Event first, per `event-payloads.md`.

doc-on-this-page.purpose: The "On this page" rail: the page's own headings, the active one lit, nested headings indented under their parent — followed by the rail's complementary groups (the repository, the community). The rail is a single path that bends inward as the outline nests, and the active marker is a dash cut from that same path, so moving between headings slides the marker **along** the line, through the bends, rather than jumping a separate bar between two positions.
useWhen: Beside the body of a long documentation page, as in-page navigation over its `h2`/`h3` outline.
To carry a page's peer links (repository, community) under the outline, each as its own named group.
avoidWhen: Expecting it to track scroll. It is presentation only: `activeId` is a prop, because the page owns the scroll container and therefore owns which heading is active.
For navigation _between_ pages — that is `DocPagination` at the foot, or the sidebar.
For an outline deeper than a couple of levels; the indent is legible for two, not for five.
related: DocPageHeader` — the masthead above the body, whose `h1` is chrome, so the outline starts at `h2`.
DocPagination` — navigation between documents, where this is navigation within one.
use-heading-nav` — the composable a page uses to receive a rail activation and scroll its own container.
bestPractices: Feed it depth 2 and 3 only; the rail indents each level by 8px and a third level reads as noise.
Own the active heading in the page (a scroll-spy) and pass it down; do not expect the rail to guess.
Keep the complementary groups to peers of the page, never sections of it — a reader must not read "Join us on Discord" as part of what they are reading.

examples.name: Default
examples.summary: Change `activeId` in the controls and watch the marker travel along the rail rather than jump — it is a dash cut from the same path the rail draws.

examples.name: Nesting
examples.summary: The rail bends between levels as the outline nests, and each level change is split into two half-curves meeting exactly on the boundary — which is what makes the marker measurable to the pixel. The complementary groups below are drawn as peers of the outline, not entries in it: no rail, no indent, no marker, and each its own named landmark, so a reader never reads "Discord" as a section of the page.

props.name: title
props.doc: The page title.

props.name: description
props.doc: The deck under the title.

props.name: breadcrumb
props.doc: Ancestor trail, current page last.

props.name: lastUpdated
props.doc: When the page's content last changed. ISO date, or a ready-made string.

props.name: metaActions
props.doc: The controls on the meta line, in reading order.

events.name: meta-action
events.notes: Fired when a meta-line control is activated; `item` is the entry that was picked. Event first, per `event-payloads.md`. A link's default navigation is the consumer's to keep or to prevent.

slots.name: breadcrumb
slots.notes: The trail; replaces the built-in `Breadcrumb` fed by the `breadcrumb` prop.

slots.name: title
slots.notes: The page's name; replaces the built-in `h1`, for a title that is more than a string.

slots.name: actions
slots.notes: A control on the title's line. Empty by default; the meta line carries the page's actions.

slots.name: details
slots.notes: Rows between the deck and the meta line — a page's own facts, tags or references.

doc-page-header.purpose: The masthead of a documentation page: where the reader is (the breadcrumb), what the page is (the title), what they can do with it (a Copy Page control that hands the page to an AI tool — or, through the `actions` slot, the consumer's own menu; the trail is likewise slottable, for an application whose crumbs route rather than navigate), the deck that says what they will have by the end, and when the content last changed. It closes on a rule spanning the column, which is what gives every `h2` below it something to be subordinate to.
useWhen: At the top of any documentation or changelog page, above `DocProse`.
avoidWhen: For an application screen's title — that is `PageHeading`, which carries console actions rather than a Copy Page control.
For a section heading inside a page — the content's own `h2` does that, and the masthead's `h1` is chrome.
related: DocProse` — the body below it. The masthead's `h1` is chrome, so authored content starts at `h2`.
DocOnThisPage` — the rail beside the body, which lists those `h2`s.
Button` / `Tooltip` / `Separator` — the meta line's entries: a quiet `text` button (an anchor when the entry has an `href`), the sentence its label has no room for, and the rule between two of them.
bestPractices: Give every `metaActions` entry a `tip`: two or three words name a control, and only a sentence says what it does.
Give an entry an `href` when it has a destination, so it is a real link — then prevent the default in `meta-action` if the app routes in-page.
Let `lastUpdated` come from the page's own frontmatter. It is the author's claim that the content changed, not the file's mtime.
Put the current page last in `breadcrumb`; it is marked as current for you.
Use `title` and `details` for a page ABOUT something (a tool, a product): its mark and maker are a title, and its facts belong between the deck and the meta line.

examples.name: Default
examples.summary: The full masthead: trail, title, deck, and the meta line. The ISO date is formatted for reading and rendered in UTC, so a bare `2026-06-30` does not become the 29th west of Greenwich.

examples.name: Actions
examples.summary: The controls are DATA, not anatomy: one array of same-shaped entries, so a site adds, drops or reorders them without touching a component. An entry with an `href` renders as a real anchor — middle-click, copy link and open-in-a-tab all work — and one without renders as a button; both report back through `meta-action`, so an app that routes in-page calls `preventDefault()` on the click it already has. Each entry carries a `tip` because the label cannot: two or three words name the control, and the sentence saying what it does appears on hover and on focus. The rules between entries are drawn only from `md` up — below that the line wraps, and a rule at the end of a wrapped line has nothing after it.
