props.name: locale
props.doc: BCP 47 locale of everything below the provider; picks the built-in catalog (`en`, `pt-BR`, `es`) and the `Intl` formats.

props.name: messages
props.doc: Partial catalog deep-merged over the built-in one, keyed by component group (`{ pagination: { next: 'Seguinte' } }`).

props.name: dir
props.doc: Text direction of the subtree; `auto` derives it from the locale (`ar`, `he`, `fa`, `ur` are right-to-left).

slots.name: default
slots.notes: The app, or the part of it that shares this locale.

webkit-provider.purpose: Sets the language and text direction of every WebKit component below it. It wraps the app once, at the root, with the user's BCP 47 locale: components then read their built-in strings (close buttons, pagination, empty states, assistive labels) from the locale catalog and format dates, numbers, file sizes, relative times and plurals with `Intl` for that locale. With no provider mounted every component falls back to English. The element it renders carries `lang` and `dir`.
useWhen: Once at the root of every app, with the locale the user chose (`pt-BR`, `en`, `es`).
Around one region that must read in another language than the rest of the page (a preview of an email in the customer's language).
To rename a built-in string for the whole app (`messages`), instead of passing the same label prop to every instance.
avoidWhen: Translating your own product copy (titles, descriptions, button labels you pass in) → keep it in your app's own i18n; the provider only covers the strings WebKit ships.
Changing one instance's label → pass the component's label prop (`aria-label`, `confirm-label`); a prop always wins over the catalog.
Only flipping the layout for a right-to-left language → still use the provider with that locale; `dir` follows it.
related: use-locale` — the composable components use to read the active locale, translate a key and format with `Intl`; use it in your own components to match WebKit's formatting.
pagination` — reads its labels and the "Showing x to y of z" line from the catalog.
confirm-dialog` — reads Confirm and Cancel from the catalog when no label is passed.
bestPractices: Mount one `WebkitProvider` at the app root and pass the locale the user chose; do not nest one per page.
Use a full BCP 47 tag (`pt-BR`, not `pt`); a tag with no built-in catalog falls back to the same language, then to English.
Override built-in strings through `messages` (partial, deep-merged), not by forking components.
Leave `dir` on `auto`: Arabic, Hebrew, Persian and Urdu locales turn the subtree right-to-left.

architecture-tabs.purpose: The architecture band of a product page: a horizontal section title with one large button, over a row of up to five tabs whose active tab draws its named diagram the full width of the frame. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'architecture-tabs', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `section-module`, `section-title`, `button`, `frame-box`, `media-tabs` and `diagram`. The tabs advance on a timer that pauses under the pointer or keyboard focus and never runs under reduced motion; that state is owned by `media-tabs`.
useWhen: To plot several architectures of one product, or one request across the platform, one diagram at a time.
avoidWhen: For features shown by an illustration each → use `feature-tabs`.
For a scroll-driven walkthrough → use `feature-scroll`.
related: media-tabs` — the timed tab row this section renders through.
diagram` — the named architecture diagram each tab draws.
bestPractices: Keep to five tabs with `position` `top` or `bottom`, three with `left` or `right`; tabs past the limit are not rendered.
Give every tab a `diagram` from the diagram library and a stable `value`.

article-body.purpose: The reading page of an article. A brand banner sits over a three-column grid: the share, community and copy-page rail on the left; the breadcrumb, headline, byline and prose down the middle at a reading measure; and the "On this page" outline on the right. Both rails stick under the header and fold away below `lg`, leaving the column alone. The section opens the page itself, so it carries its own `section-container` instead of sitting in the page column. The prose arrives as markdown: blank-line separated blocks render as `##` / `###` headings (each with an id slugged from its text, feeding the outline), `-` lists and paragraphs. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'article-body', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `section-container`, `section-module`, `frame-box`, `breadcrumb`, `hero-title`, `divider`, `doc-prose`, `tooltip`, `icon-button`, `split-button` and `doc-on-this-page`; copying to the clipboard is local behaviour.

For a closing row of related articles → use `article-cards`.

doc-on-this-page` — the outline rail fed by the body's headings.
bestPractices: Write the body as plain blocks — headings, paragraphs and `-` lists separated by blank lines; inline markdown is rendered as text.

closing-call-to-action.purpose: The last ask at the end of a landing page, followed by a hatched closing frame with no rules of its own, because the site footer under it opens with one. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'closing-call-to-action', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `section-module`, `call-to-action`, `button`, `frame-box` and `texture-material`. `kind` picks the layout only: `split` sets the headline and the primary action in a raised lead cell beside an aside cell carrying the description and the secondary action, over a tall closing frame; `panel` sets the copy and its actions on one surface, over a short closing frame; `primary` is the loud close, one centred ask on the canvas under a pixelated texture whose waves keep travelling, over a tall closing frame. All three take the same copy and the same two actions.
useWhen: To close a solution or product page on its one or two asks (`split`), or a page such as Careers on one action (`panel`), or a page that ends on its one loud ask (`primary`).
avoidWhen: For a newsletter sign-up close → use `closing-call-to-action-newsletter`.
For an ask in the middle of a page → compose `call-to-action` directly.
related: call-to-action` — the framed band this section renders.
closing-call-to-action-newsletter` — the closing band whose ask is a subscribe form.
bestPractices: Place it last on the page, right above `site-footer`, after a hatched `section-gap`.
Set `anchor: 'contact'` so the page's contact links scroll to the close.
In `split`, keep `title` and `titleMuted` to one short line each; `panel` and `primary` do not draw `titleMuted`, and `primary` does not draw `eyebrow`.

closing-call-to-action-agents.purpose: The close for a reader who may be a person or an agent: one centred ask in the loud `primary` register of the call to action, under a pixelated, waving texture, with a small segmented switch under the title that picks the way in. Each audience carries an optional copyable line and its actions; under them, a line types its words one after another behind a blinking cursor, then a closing sentence, both the same for every audience so the band keeps its height when the switch changes. The hatched closing frame follows. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'closing-call-to-action-agents', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `section-module`, `call-to-action`, `toggle-group`, `input-group`, `copy-button`, `button`, `frame-box` and `texture-material`. The switch and the typed word are local state.
useWhen: To close a developer page whose reader may be a person or the person's agent.
avoidWhen: For a close on one or two link actions → use `closing-call-to-action` (`primary` for the same loud register without the switch).
For a newsletter sign-up → use `closing-call-to-action-newsletter`.
related: closing-call-to-action` — the same close without the audience switch.
bestPractices: Keep two audiences; the first one opens.
Keep each copyable line short enough to fit the field; the copy button copies exactly what it shows.
Keep `typedWords` to a few short words; screen readers and reduced motion get the whole list at once.

closing-call-to-action-newsletter.purpose: The closing band whose ask is a newsletter sign-up: the overline and a large headline on the lead side, a subscribe form labelled by the ask on the other, over a strip lit by the pixelated primary wave, then the hatched closing frame. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'closing-call-to-action-newsletter', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `section-module`, `frame-box`, `overline`, `field`, `input`, `button` and `texture-material`. The block never sends: it validates the address locally (an empty field and a malformed address each show their message under the field) and on a valid submit emits `submit` with the event and `{ email }`; the site posts the address and reports the outcome back through `loading`, `submitted` and `error`, which the band renders with the messages from `form`.
useWhen: To close the Blog or the Resource Hub on a newsletter subscription.
avoidWhen: For a close on one or two link actions → use `closing-call-to-action`.
For a lead form with several fields → use `hero-form`.
related: closing-call-to-action` — the closing band whose ask is a link action.
message` — renders the success and failure messages.
bestPractices: Set `loading` while the address is sent, then `submitted` or `error` with the outcome.
Keep `description` to one sentence; it is set as the large headline.
Write `form.invalidMessage` with an example address so the fix is obvious.

code-split.purpose: The claim-beside-its-code band of a product page: a framed media split whose copy states the claim, with one or two large buttons under it, and whose media is a code sample on the pixelate texture, cut off by the frame's bottom rule. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'code-split', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `section-module`, `media-split`, `code-block` and `button`. One tab draws a filename bar; several draw a tab strip, and a tab that carries an `icon` shows that mark beside its label.
useWhen: When the argument of a product page is a config file or a handler a developer can read, like Functions, Application Accelerator or AI Gateway.
avoidWhen: For a terminal session under a headline → use `cli-terminal`.
For a run of capabilities, each with its own sample, pinned while the page scrolls → use `sticky-scroll-code`.

code-block` — the tabbed code sample in the media cell.
bestPractices: Keep the sample short enough to read in the cell; the frame cuts off whatever runs past it.
Give every tab a `code`; a tab without one is skipped.
Use `primaryAction` alone for one destination, and add `secondaryAction` only for a second, distinct one.

comparison-table.purpose: The capability-by-capability comparison of Azion with one competitor on a migration landing page: a left section title over a framed table whose header row (the capability column, the Azion brand and the competitor logo) stays pinned while the page scrolls. avoidWhen: To compare Azion's own plans → use `compare-plans`.

faq-section.purpose: The frequently asked questions band near the end of a landing page: the heading in the left column and the questions on the right, each answer closed until the reader opens it, one at a time. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'faq-section', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `section-module` and `faq`. An answer is a markdown string, so it can run to several paragraphs (split by a blank line) and `- ` bullet lists, and a sentence can carry a link, bold or italic text, all without a slot or `v-html`.
useWhen: To answer the handful of questions a reader still has before the closing call to action.
avoidWhen: For answers that need content beyond paragraphs, bullet lists and inline links (tables, images, code) → compose `faq` with its `answer` slot.
For a single highlighted question with an action → use `call-to-action`.
related: faq` — the framed accordion band this section renders.
closing-call-to-action` — the band that usually follows it.
bestPractices: Use one FAQ section per page and give it `anchor: 'faq'` so a page can link straight to it.
Keep an answer short; links use `[label](href)`, bold `**text**` and italic `*text*`.
Separate paragraphs with a blank line; start each bullet with `- ` and keep the list in its own block.
Absolute `https://` links open in a new tab; site-relative links stay in the tab.

feature-scroll.purpose: The walkthrough band of a product page: a large section title over one screen per feature. From the large breakpoint up the features scroll through a sticky stack — the copy advances while the illustration stays pinned in a framed, textured stage with one small action under each step; below it the same features are a three-column grid of media tiles. avoidWhen: For three reasons with no scroll story → use `feature-tiles`.

related: sticky-stack` — the scroll engine the large layout runs on.
media-tile` — the cell the small layout renders each feature with.
bestPractices: Four to six items; the stack needs enough steps to earn the scroll.
Give every item an `illustration`; it is the pinned picture on large screens and the tile media on small ones.
Keep `action` to a short label such as "Docs" — it sits under the step copy at the small size.

feature-tiles.purpose: The reasons band of a marketing page: an optional centered section title over a frame grid of media tiles, each an image or an illustration above a short heading and a sentence. useWhen: To state three or four reasons to buy, each with a picture, under a product or pricing argument.
avoidWhen: For linked use cases → use `use-case-links`.
For a scroll-driven walkthrough with one screen per feature → use `feature-scroll`.
related: media-tile` — the picture-over-copy cell each tile is rendered with.
feature-widgets` — the sibling band whose cells carry an action each.
bestPractices: Match the tile count to the kind: four tiles for `artwork`, three for `illustrated`.
Give a tile either `image` (a URL) or `illustration` (a registry name), not both; `scale` only matters with `illustration`.
Leave `title` empty to drop the header when the band sits under a hero that already states it; set `anchor` when a link above scrolls to the band.

hero-band.purpose: The opening band of a marketing page: the page `h1` with its overline, accent phrase, sentence and up to two actions, full width above the page column, with an optional client strip on the floor. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'hero-band', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `hero`, `hero-title`, `button` and `illustration`. `kind` picks the layout only: `centered` fills a screen over a dot field with the copy centered, `title-band` is a padded band with the copy centered, `pixel-floor` sets the copy at the start over an animated pixel floor, and `copy-beside-art` sets an illustration beside the copy; every layout takes the same copy, actions and client strip.
useWhen: To open a home, solution, product, listing or contact page with its headline and main actions.
avoidWhen: For a hero followed by a grid of arguments → use `hero-with-opening`.
For a hero with a topology scene under the copy → use `hero-copy-on-top-art`.
For a band inside the page column → use `section-module` or a sibling section.
related: hero` — the band primitive every layout is rendered with.
hero-title` — the headline block rendered inside it.
bestPractices: Use `title-band` with `size="large"` for a product page and `size="medium"` for a page whose bands start right under the headline.
Give `illustration` and `illustrationAriaLabel` only to the `copy-beside-art` layout; the other layouts ignore them.
Set `headerOffset` to the height of the site header so a band that fills a screen fills exactly the first screen with it.

It is a separate section from `hero-band` because the scene is a data model of its own: levels of cards, each with a status and an optional focus.
useWhen: To open a product page whose object is best shown as a small topology (domains feeding a workload that binds an application and a firewall).
avoidWhen: For an opening band with no scene → use `hero-band`.

related: hero-band` — the sibling opening band with the same copy and actions and no scene.
flow` — the diagram primitive the scene is rendered with.
bestPractices: Keep three levels of one or two cards so the scene fits the column on a tablet.
Mark exactly one card `lit`, the focus of the scene.

hero-form.purpose: The opening band of a lead-capture page, where the form is the reason for the page: the hero copy and a list of highlights on one side, the form on the other, above the fold, with the client strip on the floor. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'hero-form', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `hero`, `hero-title`, `topic`, `field`, `input`, `select`, `phone-input`, `textarea`, `button` and `message`. The fields are data: each entry of `fields` picks its control by `kind`, so the Contact page and the Under attack page are the same block with different `fields`. The block never sends: it validates the fields locally (required fields and the email format, with the messages from `messages`) and on a valid submit emits `submit` with the event and the values keyed by field `name`; the site posts them and reports the outcome back through `loading`, `submitted` and `error`.
useWhen: To open a page whose purpose is a lead form, such as Contact sales or Under attack.
avoidWhen: For a newsletter sign-up with one email field → use `closing-call-to-action-newsletter`.
For an opening band with calls to action and no form → use `hero-band` or `hero-with-opening`.
related: closing-call-to-action-newsletter` — the other form section; same `submit` and state contract.
message` — renders the success and failure messages.
bestPractices: Give every field a unique `name`; it is the key of the submitted value.
Mark half-width fields in pairs so each row stays full.
Set `loading` while the values are sent, then `submitted` or `error` with the outcome.

hero-with-opening.purpose: The opening band of a product page followed straight by its arguments: a large centered title band with the page `h1`, overline, sentence and up to two actions, then a frame grid of three-column argument cells in the page column, closed by a hatched gap. useWhen: To open a product page that argues on three or six claims right under its headline.
avoidWhen: For an opening band with no arguments → use `hero-band`.
For a reasons band further down the page → use `feature-tiles` or `use-cases`.
related: hero-band` — the opening band without the argument grid.
topic` — the icon, heading and sentence each argument is rendered with.
bestPractices: Use three or six items so every row of the grid is full.
Keep each item to a short title and one sentence.
A title longer than 45 characters widens the headline column so it breaks into two lines instead of three.

props.name: anchor
props.doc: In-page `id` of the band, the target of a `#hash` link.

props.name: title
props.doc: Headline over the listing, rendered by the section title as its `h2` and naming the band.

props.name: columns
props.doc: The columns, left to right; each is `{ key, label, grow?, align? }`. The first names the row and links it, the second describes it on phones.

props.name: rows
props.doc: Every row, in source order; each is `{ href, group, values, facets }` where `values` and `facets` are keyed by column and facet.

props.name: groups
props.doc: The groups the rows are listed under, in order; a group with no matching row is not shown.

props.name: facets
props.doc: The facet selects; each is `{ key, label, allLabel, options }` where `key` matches a row facet and seeds it from `?key=` in the URL, and every option is `{ value, label }`.

props.name: sorts
props.doc: The orders, the first the default; each is `{ value, label, by? }` where `by` is the column it sorts on and an empty `by` keeps the source order.

props.name: sortAriaLabel
props.doc: Accessible name of the order select.

props.name: search
props.doc: The search field; `{ placeholder, shortPlaceholder, label }` where `shortPlaceholder` is used below the large breakpoint and `label` names the field. Omitted when absent.

props.name: empty
props.doc: The state shown when nothing matches; `{ title, description, clearLabel }` where `clearLabel` is the button that clears the search and every facet. Omitted when absent.

listing-browser.purpose: The full, browsable listing of a page such as the Careers jobs list: a headline over a toolbar (a search field, one select per facet and one for the order) and every row under its group, as a table from the small breakpoint up and as a list of items below it, with an empty state when nothing matches. Search, facets and order are local state over the rows the page carries; a facet is seeded from `?<key>=` in the URL when the value is one the page offers. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'listing-browser', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — so its whole API is the props below, and it composes `section-module`, `section-title`, `frame-box`, `input`, `select`, `table`, `item`, `empty-state` and `button` rather than owning any anatomy of its own.
useWhen: For a listing a reader narrows by text and by a few facets, such as open positions grouped by department.
When every row links to its own page and the listing fits in the page JSON.
avoidWhen: For a short, unfiltered preview of the same rows → use `listing-table`.
For a data table with sorting, selection and pagination inside the product → use `table`.
For a grid of linked topic cards → use `subject-library`.
related: table` — the composed rows and cells the listing renders from the small breakpoint up.
item` — the list rows the listing renders below the small breakpoint.
empty-state` — the state shown when the search and facets match nothing.
bestPractices: Name the first column after what the row is (`Role`); it is the row's link, and the second column describes the row on phones.
Give every row the facet values it carries under the facet's `key`, so the selects narrow it.
Keep `groups` in the order the reader scans; rows of a group not listed there are not shown.
Make the first entry of `sorts` the order the page is authored in, with an empty `by`.

listing-table.purpose: A titled preview of a longer listing: a few linked rows in columns, and one outlined button into the full list. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'listing-table', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `section-module`, `section-title`, `frame-box`, `table` and, below `sm`, `item`. Each row is one link named by its first column; the whole row is clickable with the pointer and the first column's link is the keyboard and screen-reader path. Below `sm` the same rows become a list of items, the first column as the title and the second as the description, with the button going full width.
useWhen: To preview the latest entries of a listing (open roles, releases, events) with a way into the full list.
avoidWhen: For a filterable or paginated listing → use `listing-browser`.
For a comparison of plans or features → use the pricing matrix.
related: table` — the composition table the wide layout renders.
listing-browser` — the full listing this band links into.
bestPractices: Keep three columns at most; the first names the row and the second describes it on phones.
Give the wide columns `grow: 2` and align a short trailing column to `end`.
Keep the preview to a handful of rows and point `primaryAction` at the full listing.

media-split-band.purpose: One claim beside its picture, on its own frame: the copy cell with its overline, headline and sentence on one side, and the media on a raised, pixel-textured surface on the other. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'media-split-band', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `section-module`, a framed `media-split`, `button`, `illustration` and the webkit scene assets. The media is a scene, an image or an illustration; with one action the whole band links to it, with two the band stays unlinked.
useWhen: To make one point beside one picture and move on (a values statement, a single product claim).
avoidWhen: For several claims stacked one after the other → use `media-split-stack`.
For a claim beside a code sample → use `code-split`.
related: media-split` — the band primitive the section is rendered with.
media-split-stack` — the stacked sibling for a run of claims.
bestPractices: Give the band exactly one media: `scene`, `image` or `illustration`; when several are set the first of that order wins.
Use `size="large"` for a band that carries only its headline and description.
Give an `image` its `width` and `height` so the page reserves its box before it loads.

media-split-stack.purpose: A run of large media-split bands that pile up under the site header as the page scrolls, each a centered claim with an outlined "learn more" button beside its picture, the whole band linking through. An optional large centered section title opens the run. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'media-split-stack', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `section-module`, `section-title`, `band-stack`, `media-split`, `illustration` and `button`. `kind` picks the layout only: `media-end` sets every picture at the closing end, `alternating` starts it at the opening end and swaps sides band by band; the bands keep the same shape in both.
useWhen: To list the solution areas or the claims of a page, one large band each, with a link through to its own page.
avoidWhen: For a single claim beside its media → use `media-split` directly.
For small reasons in a grid → use `feature-tiles`.
related: band-stack` — the sticky run the bands pile up in.
media-split` — the band each entry renders through.
bestPractices: Give a band either `image` (a URL, with `imageAlt` when it says something) or `illustration` (a registry name, with `illustrationLabel`), not both; a band with neither renders without its media cell.
Give every band an `action`; it is both the button and the link the whole band follows.

network-section.purpose: The infrastructure band of a marketing page: a tall framed panel with the world network map drawn behind a small left-aligned title, a lead line and a row of claim chips, closed by a floor of either client outcomes (a quote with its highlights and the client's mark) or benefits (icon-led topics). quote` / `topic` — the two cell types the floor renders.

platform-directory.purpose: A directory of Azion's products under a section title: one column per product group (Build, Store, Secure, Observe), each row an icon, a product name and one line about it, linking to that product. avoidWhen: For a handful of icon-led use cases → use `use-cases`.

related: column-navigation` — the named navigation landmark whose columns and rows this band fills.
section-title` — the headline over the directory.

Give each item an `href`; an item without a title or a link is skipped, and a group left with no items is skipped too.
Set `ariaLabel` so the directory's navigation landmark is told apart from the site navigation.

site-footer.purpose: The footer under every marketing page: the link columns, then the social row beside the status indicator and the language select. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'site-footer', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `footer`, `brand`, `icon-button`, `status-indicator` and `select`. From `lg` the Azion mark leads the social row; below it the mark moves to the footer's signature band, so the icons get the row to themselves. The language select keeps its own value locally; its options are the labels the reader sees.
useWhen: As the last block of every marketing page.
avoidWhen: Inside the product console or the docs → compose `footer` directly.
For a closing ask above the footer → use `closing-call-to-action`.
related: footer` — the composition footer this section fills.
closing-call-to-action` — the band that sits right above it.
bestPractices: Use `kind: 'site'` under a framed marketing page, so the footer draws the page frame and closes on its bottom rule; the page above must not draw a bottom rule of its own.
Keep four link columns so the grid fills at `md`.
Give every social link a `label` that names the network, since the button shows only the glyph.

props.name: menus
props.doc: The mega-menus, in bar order; each is `{ value, label, columns }` where `columns` is an array of columns, each holding groups of `{ label, href?, items }` and each item `{ label, description?, href?, icon? }`.

props.name: links
props.doc: Bar entries that open no panel, after the menus; each is `{ label, href }`.

props.name: contact
props.doc: Contact link set in the bar from `xl` up and last in the sheet's tree; `{ label, href }`.

props.name: primaryAction
props.doc: The sign-up button, filled, in the bar and in the sheet footer; `{ label, href }`.

props.name: secondaryAction
props.doc: The login button beside it, in the bar and in the sheet footer; `{ label, href }`.

site-nav.purpose: The marketing site's own navigation: a sticky bar with the Azion mark, the mega-menu triggers and plain links, and the contact, login and sign-up actions, plus the sheet that carries the same tree below `xl`. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'site-nav', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `global-header`, `brand`, `navigation-menu`, `icon-button`, `button`, `drawer`, `panel-header`, `panel-footer`, `scroll-area` and `menu`. Each mega-menu lists its panel as columns of groups, and the sheet's drill-down tree is projected from the same menus, so an entry added to a panel is in both. The open state of the sheet, its drill path and the bar's inline inset are local state.
useWhen: At the top of every marketing page, once.
avoidWhen: For the Console's application header → use `global-header` directly.
For an in-page list of links → use `navigation-menu` or `menu` directly.
related: global-header` — the bar primitive the navigation is rendered in.
navigation-menu` — the mega-menu the bar opens from `xl` up.
menu` — the drill-down tree the sheet carries below `xl`.
bestPractices: Keep a panel to one, two or four columns; only the four-column panel is stretched to the page column.
Stack a short group under another in the same column (Platform under Observe) instead of adding a fifth column.
Give every entry an `href`; an entry without one links to `#`.

props.name: items
props.doc: The figures rendered as cells, in order; each item is `{ value, label, prefix?, suffix? }` where `value` is the figure, `label` its caption, and `prefix` / `suffix` the qualifier and unit set beside it.

stats-band.purpose: The proof-by-numbers band of a marketing page: a framed row of big figures, each with its caption and optional prefix or unit. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'stats-band', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `section-module`, `frame-box` and `big-numbers`, which owns the figures' scale and layout.
useWhen: To state reach, scale or results in three to five figures right after a hero or a claim.
avoidWhen: For figures that need a quote or a logo beside them → use `network-section` or `logo-wall-quote`.
For a single figure inside another band → use `big-numbers` directly.
related: big-numbers` — the figure row this band frames.
network-section` — the band that pairs claims with client outcomes.
bestPractices: Keep `value` short and the unit in `suffix`, so the figure reads at a glance.
Three to five items; more than that and the figures stop reading as a band.

sticky-scroll-code.purpose: The developer-capabilities band of a product page: a large section title over a sticky stack whose claims scroll past a pinned media frame, the open claim showing its one-file code sample on the pixelate texture and its own button under its description. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'sticky-scroll-code', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `section-module`, `section-title`, `frame-box`, `sticky-stack`, `texture-material`, `code-block` and `button`. Which claim is open is scroll-driven state owned by `sticky-stack`.
useWhen: To walk a developer through several capabilities, each proven by a short file, while the page scrolls.
avoidWhen: For one claim beside one sample → use `code-split`.
For a walkthrough shown by illustrations → use `feature-scroll`.
related: sticky-stack` — the pinned, scroll-driven run of claims this section renders through.
code-block` — the one-file sample each claim shows.
bestPractices: Keep each sample short enough to read in the pinned frame.
Give every item a `code`; the item's `action` is optional and shows only while the item is open.

<script setup>
  import StickyScrollCode from '@aziontech/webkit/sticky-scroll-code'

  const items = [
    {
      title: 'Automated deployment via Git or CLI',
      description:
        'Run one command from the project you already have, or connect the repository and let every push to the branch ship itself.',
      action: {
        label: 'Docs',
        href: 'https://www.azion.com/en/documentation/devtools/',
        trailing: true
      },
      code: {
        fileName: 'deploy.sh',
        fileIcon: 'ai ai-azion-cli',
        language: 'bash',
        code: '# Ship the project in front of you\nazion deploy\n\n# Or link the repo once, and every push to main deploys\nazion link --preset next\ngit push origin main\n\n# Then roll back if it should not have gone out\nazion rollback --to previous',
        copyAriaLabel: 'Copy the deploy.sh sample'
      }
    },
    {
      title: 'Compatibility with modern web frameworks',
      description:
        'Next, Nuxt, Astro, Svelte and twenty more build through a preset the CLI detects, so the config file stays this short.',
      action: {
        label: 'Docs',
        href: 'https://www.azion.com/en/documentation/devtools/',
        trailing: true
      },
      code: {
        fileName: 'azion.config.js',
        fileIcon: 'ai-cor ai-js',
        language: 'javascript',
        code: "import { defineConfig } from 'azion'\n\nexport default defineConfig({\n  build: {\n    entry: 'src/index.ts',\n    worker: true,\n    preset: 'next'\n  },\n  functions: [\n    { name: 'storefront', path: '.edge/worker.js' }\n  ]\n})",
        copyAriaLabel: 'Copy the azion.config.js sample'
      }
    },
    {
      title: 'APIs for automation and integration',
      description:
        'Everything the console does is a call you can make yourself, so a workload can be created by the pipeline that needed it.',
      action: {
        label: 'Docs',
        href: 'https://www.azion.com/en/documentation/devtools/',
        trailing: true
      },
      code: {
        fileName: 'create-workload.sh',
        fileIcon: 'ai ai-azion-cli',
        language: 'bash',
        code: '# Create the workload the pipeline just built for\ncurl -X POST https://api.azion.com/v4/workloads \\\n  -H "Authorization: Token $AZION_TOKEN" \\\n  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \\\n  -d \'{\n    "name": "storefront",\n    "domains": ["storefront.example.com"]\n  }\'',
        copyAriaLabel: 'Copy the create-workload.sh sample'
      }
    },
    {
      title: 'Infrastructure as code with Terraform',
      description:
        'Declare workloads, applications and domains in the provider and apply them under the same review as the rest of your estate.',
      action: {
        label: 'Docs',
        href: 'https://www.azion.com/en/documentation/devtools/',
        trailing: true
      },
      code: {
        fileName: 'main.tf',
        fileIcon: 'ai-cor ai-terraform',
        language: 'hcl',
        code: 'resource "azion_application" "storefront" {\n  name                    = "storefront"\n  edge_functions          = true\n  application_accelerator = true\n}\n\nresource "azion_workload" "storefront" {\n  name    = "storefront"\n  domains = ["storefront.example.com"]\n\n  application {\n    id = azion_application.storefront.id\n  }\n}',
        copyAriaLabel: 'Copy the main.tf sample'
      }
    },
    {
      title: 'Metrics and events via GraphQL API',
      description:
        'Query the same numbers the console charts, from one endpoint, so a dashboard you already run can carry the platform too.',
      action: {
        label: 'Docs',
        href: 'https://www.azion.com/en/documentation/devtools/',
        trailing: true
      },
      code: {
        fileName: 'requests.graphql',
        fileIcon: 'ai-cor ai-graphql',
        language: 'graphql',
        code: 'query RequestsByStatus($begin: DateTime!, $end: DateTime!) {\n  httpMetrics(\n    limit: 100\n    filter: { tsRange: { begin: $begin, end: $end } }\n    groupBy: [status]\n  ) {\n    status\n    requests: sum(field: requests)\n    p95: percentile(field: requestTime, percentile: 95)\n  }\n}',
        copyAriaLabel: 'Copy the requests.graphql sample'
      }
    }
  ]
</script>

<template>
  <StickyScrollCode
    eyebrow="Ship It"
    title="Everything You Need to Build and Deploy"
    description="Deploy from Git or the CLI, automate with APIs and Terraform, and query every metric over GraphQL. One platform carries your web app from the first push to the traffic it serves."
    :items="items"
  />
</template>

story-library.purpose: Every success story of a company as one filterable library. A left-aligned title sits over a toolbar — a search field and one searchable select per facet (industry, solution, product) on one row — then a grid of story cards and a load-more button. Each card is one link named by its company: the client mark in a single ink, the story's category as an overline, its description and a read cue whose arrow nudges on hover. The grid runs one column on phones, two from `sm` and three from `lg`. Search and facets combine; when nothing matches, an empty state offers to clear every filter. It is a page section — the site places it from a `{ _id: 'story-library', props }` entry and binds `props` straight onto it — and it composes `section-module`, `section-title`, `frame-box`, `input`, `select`, `button` and `empty-state`; the search, the facet selections and each select's own option search are local state.
useWhen: To list every success story with search and facet filters.
avoidWhen: For a closing row of three related stories → use `article-cards`.
For a filterable list of articles → use `article-index-blog` or `article-index-resource-hub`.
related: article-index-resource-hub` — the sibling listing of articles with facet dropdowns.
empty-state` — the no-match state.
bestPractices: Derive each facet's `options` from the values the items carry, so every option matches at least one story.
Give every item a `facets` entry per facet `key`; an item without one never matches a selection on that facet.

props.name: kind
props.doc: Register of the grid: gutters between self-contained cards, hairline rules drawn by the gaps, or framed cells that draw their own rules and marks.

props.name: columns
props.doc: How many columns the grid fans out to at the large breakpoint.

props.name: mobileColumns
props.doc: How many columns the grid holds below the small breakpoint.

props.name: dividerColor
props.doc: Weight of the hairline rules in the `divider` register.

props.name: flush
props.doc: In the `frame` register, the surrounding frame already draws the grid's outer rules: the grid drops its own top and left ones and lays its right and bottom ones onto the frame's, so a framed column keeps one hairline per edge.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: The cells, in reading order. In the `frame` register they are `CardGrid.Cell` elements; in the `divider` register each cell fills its own background.

card-grid.purpose: The responsive cell grid of the page language, in three registers: spaced cards separated by real gutters, a hairline box grid whose internal rules are the gaps themselves, and a framed grid whose cells are real `frame-box` elements. The `frame` register is the one that composes: each `CardGrid.Cell` draws its own rules and corner marks and carries its own fill, so the grid needs no background trick and nests flush inside a column that already owns the outer edges.
useWhen: For a row or block of equal cells that should fan out from one column on a phone to several on a wide screen.
With `kind` set to `frame` whenever the cells are real content — a `topic`, a claim, a figure — and should carry the page's frame language, corner marks included.
For the hairline cell grid a `section-module` body holds, with `kind` set to `divider`.
For a row of self-contained cards with gutters between them, with the default `gap`.
avoidWhen: For a mosaic whose cells claim different numbers of columns and rows → use `bento-grid`, which is this grid with spans.
For a single framed box → use `frame-box`.
For one card with a header, content and footer → use `card`.
For the band that wraps the grid → use `section-module`.
For tabular data a reader scans row by row → use `table`.
related: bento-grid` — the same framed grid with unequal cells; reach for it when one claim deserves more room than the rest.
topic` — the glyph, headline and sentence a `frame` cell usually holds.
section-module` — the band whose body holds this grid.
section-container` — the column whose vertical rules the `divider` and flush `frame` grids deliberately do not repeat.
frame-box` — the frame each `frame` cell is drawn with, and the framed box a `gap` cell may be built from.
card` — a padded card surface, the usual child of a `gap` grid.
bestPractices: Prefer `frame` over `divider` for new work. The hairline register depends on every child filling its own background; the framed register draws real rules, so a cell that forgets its fill still reads correctly, and the corner marks come with it.
Give every child of a `divider` grid its own background fill, or the gap trick has nothing to show through and the whole band goes the colour of the rule.

Leave the perimeter to the container: the `divider` register draws no outer border, and a `frame` grid set to `flush` withholds its own top and left rules so a surrounding `frame-box` keeps one hairline per edge.
Let the grid draw the rules. Do not add borders inside a `frame` cell, or the shared edges double.
Give a cell `kind="none"` and `:padded="false"` when its own content paints the cell — a media layer, a brand fill, or a link that must be the whole tile.
Reach for `mobileColumns` of `2` only for short, glyph-led cells; a cell carrying a description reads better one-up on a phone.

props.name: kind
props.doc: Which texture to paint; `none` renders the layer with no texture at all.

props.name: size
props.doc: Pitch of the tiling — how far apart the cells sit.

props.name: fade
props.doc: Fades the layer out along an axis so it meets content without a hard edge.

texture-material.purpose: The one decorative surface every band in the system is painted on: a full-bleed, non-interactive layer that tiles a texture behind whatever sits above it. It is a material, not a container — it takes no content and claims no space, so a band composes it into its own backdrop slot and keeps ownership of its layout.
useWhen: In a band's `background` slot (`hero`), where the opening band needs the site's own lattice under its copy.
Behind a panel, dropzone or slide that would read as empty at a flat fill.
Anywhere a surface should look like a technical drawing ground without shipping an image.
avoidWhen: To draw the rules between real content cells → use `frame-box`, whose rules are structural.
For the ruled divider between sections → use `section-gap`, which composes this layer's `lines` kind and owns that treatment.
For a meaningful image or diagram → use `illustration`.
As a wrapper around content. The layer is absolutely positioned and paints only itself; content is a sibling above it, inside the positioned ancestor.
related: hero` — the band whose `background` slot this is composed into.
frame-box` — structural rules and corner marks, not decoration.
section-gap` — the hatched rhythm band between sections.
hero` — the marketing band that paints this texture behind its own copy.
bestPractices: Give the layer a positioned ancestor (`relative`) that also clips it; it fills that box and nothing else.

Keep the texture behind copy, never over it. `dots` is the quiet default; `lines` is quieter still and reads as ruled paper; `dither` and `pixelate` are loud enough to need their ink dropped or their dense end steered away from the words.
Do not stack two layers at different pitches — that reads as a moiré, not as a texture.
Quiet a texture with `--texture-ink` rather than with `opacity`, so the ground keeps showing through at full strength.
Leave it out when the band already sits inside a `frame-box`; rules plus texture is usually one layer too many.

examples.name: Default
examples.summary: The layer fills its nearest positioned ancestor, so the box it sits in is what gives it a size.

examples.name: Kinds
examples.summary: Five materials at their measured geometry. `dots` is the quiet default and `lines` the quietest — fine vertical rules whose transparency is the ink’s own, so each one stays solid edge to edge. `dither` ramps its density along an axis, and `pixelate` lights its grid from underneath with two crossing waves.

examples.name: Sizes
examples.summary: One step either side of the measured pitch. A size scales the texture whole, so the cell keeps its proportion to the lattice.

props.name: title
props.doc: The claim, rendered as the topic's heading.

props.name: description
props.doc: One sentence explaining the claim; overridden by the default slot.

props.name: icon
props.doc: Icon class for the glyph that leads the headline.

props.name: href
props.doc: When set, the whole claim renders as an anchor link to this URL and its headline closes on a trailing arrow.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: Level of the heading element. Keep `2` when the band has no headline of its own; drop it to `3` when a `section-title` has already opened the section, so the document outline stays in order.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: Description body; replaces the `description` prop when provided.

topic.purpose: One claim stated in three parts: a glyph, a short headline it shares a line with, and a sentence under them that explains it. It is the repeated unit of a marketing claim grid — the content of a cell, not the cell itself, so it carries no surface, no padding and no rules of its own and reads the same dropped into a `card-grid` cell, a `bento-grid` cell, or a column the page lays out by hand. Given an `href` the whole claim becomes the link, and its headline closes on a trailing arrow, so a band of claims needs no separate row of "learn more" controls.
useWhen: For each cell of a "what you get" band: a row of equal claims under a section's headline.
Inside `CardGrid.Cell` or `BentoGrid.Cell`, where the grid owns the frame and the fill and the topic owns only the copy.
Whenever a claim is glyph-led and one sentence long, repeated three to six times across a band.
avoidWhen: For a tile with its own border and surface → keep the topic and put it in a `CardGrid.Cell`, which draws the frame and the fill.
For a claim that carries an eyebrow, a media region or a button → use `media-split`.
For the headline that opens the whole section → use `section-title`.
For a measured figure with a unit → use `big-numbers`.
For a console list row with media and actions → use `item`.
related: card-grid` — the equal-cell grid a topic is usually repeated in; its `frame` register gives each topic a real `frame-box` cell.
bento-grid` — the unequal-cell mosaic, when one claim deserves more room than the rest.
section-title` — the headline that opens the band a row of topics sits in.
bestPractices: Let the cell own the surface. A topic paints no background and adds no padding, so put it inside `CardGrid.Cell` / `BentoGrid.Cell` (or a padded cell the page owns) rather than giving the topic a fill.

Keep `headingLevel` in step with the page outline: `2` when the band has no headline of its own and these are the first sub-headings under the `h1`, `3` when a `section-title` has already opened the section. The level is the outline; the size is fixed at `heading-xs`.
Keep the description to one sentence. The glyph carries the recognition, the headline carries the claim, and a second sentence turns a scannable grid into a wall of prose.
Drop `icon` for a band whose claims are not glyph-led rather than reaching for a decorative glyph that says nothing.

Give the claim an `href` rather than composing a button under it. A grid of six claims that each close on their own "Learn more" reads as six calls to action instead of six claims, and the button is a second target for the destination the claim already points at.

A linked claim stretches its link over the nearest positioned ancestor, so the whole cell is the hover and click target, not just the copy. `CardGrid.Cell` and `BentoGrid.Cell` are positioned; a cell the page builds by hand needs `relative`, or every claim in the grid covers the band.

examples.name: WithoutIcon
examples.summary: Without an icon the headline leads. Drop the glyph for a band whose claims are not glyph-led rather than reaching for one that says nothing.

props.name: title
props.doc: Headline of the module's header row, rendered as its `h2`.

props.name: description
props.doc: Supporting sentence under the headline.

props.name: eyebrow
props.doc: Short uppercase overline rendered above the headline.

props.name: kind
props.doc: Layout of the default header row.

props.name: divided
props.doc: Draw the top rule that divides this module from the one above it.

props.name: padded
props.doc: Pad the module's body. Leave off for an edge-to-edge grid that owns its cell padding.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: The module's body.

slots.name: header
slots.notes: Replaces the default header row entirely.

slots.name: actions
slots.notes: Trailing controls inside the default header row.

section-module.purpose: The brick of the page column: a section whose header row is divided from its body by a hairline and which is divided from the module above it by another. Stacked inside a `section-container`, a run of modules reads as one continuous frame, because each module draws only its own top rule and hands its sides to the column. It is where a band's header and a band's content are joined, so no page has to re-draw that join.
useWhen: For every band stacked inside a `section-container`.
Whenever a band needs a header row divided from its content by a rule.
For a body-only band, by passing no title and no header slot.
avoidWhen: For the full-bleed band at the top of a page → use `hero`.
For the column the modules stack inside → use `section-container`.
For the header alone, with no body → use `section-title`, which this module composes.
For a hairline grid of cells → use `card-grid` inside this module's body.
related: section-container` — the framed column this module stacks inside.
section-title` — the header row this module renders by default.
card-grid` — the edge-to-edge cell grid a module's body commonly holds.
frame-box` — the registration frame a body wraps itself in.
bestPractices: Pass `divided` as `false` on the first module in a column: its top edge is already the hero's bottom rule, and drawing its own would put two hairlines on one pixel.
Pass `padded` as `false` when the body is an edge-to-edge `card-grid`, so the grid's rules meet the frame with no gutter.
Use `title` and `eyebrow` for the ordinary header, and reach for the `header` slot only when the row needs markup the default header cannot express.

examples.name: Default
examples.summary: A header row divided from the body by one hairline. The header is a `SectionTitle`, so the module never re-implements that anatomy.

examples.name: Kinds
examples.summary: The three header layouts, stacked — they differ only in where the copy sits.

examples.name: Divided
examples.summary: Two modules, the first undivided. A shared edge is invisible on a single module — the stack is what proves the rule is drawn once.

props.name: maxWidth
props.doc: Width the column is capped at; `site` is the marketing measure every band of that page frame shares.

props.name: bordered
props.doc: Draw the column's two vertical rules.

props.name: padded
props.doc: Pad the column itself. Leave off for a stack of modules that own their padding.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: The bands stacked inside the column, in reading order.

section-container.purpose: The framed content column: a centered, width-capped block carrying only its two vertical rules, which every section below a hero stacks inside. It is the middle layer of the page language — the hero above it owns the page's top rule, the footer below it owns the bottom, and this column owns the sides — so a page's frame is drawn once, by three components, instead of by every band that happens to need an edge.
useWhen: As the container for every band below a `hero`, on a marketing, hub or documentation page.
Whenever a stack of `section-module` bricks needs one continuous frame around it.
For a plain prose column that should sit on the page's own measure, with `padded`.
avoidWhen: For the full-bleed band at the top of a page → use `hero`, which is the hero rule.
For one band inside the column → use `section-module`, the brick this container stacks.
For a hairline grid of cells → use `card-grid`, which draws its rules as gaps.
For a bordered box around arbitrary content → use `frame-box`.
related: hero` — the full-bleed opening band above this column; its `border-b` is this column's top edge.
section-module` — the brick stacked inside this column.
card-grid` — the hairline cell grid a module's body holds.
frame-box` — the registration frame a module wraps its body in.
bestPractices: Leave `padded` off for a stack of modules: each brick owns its own padding, and column padding would double it and pull the bricks off the frame.
Match `maxWidth` to the `hero` above it so the band's content and the column's content open on one vertical.
Turn `bordered` off only for a column nested inside another frame, where the outer frame already draws the sides.

examples.name: Default
examples.summary: Two bands stacked inside the column. The column draws the vertical rules; each band draws only its own horizontal ones, so no line is doubled.

examples.name: Widths
examples.summary: Three caps in one view — a width only reads against another.

examples.name: Bordered
examples.summary: With `bordered` off the column hands its sides to whatever frame encloses it.

props.name: kind
props.doc: Register of the tile: `frame` draws the page's frame around the media alone, `plain` draws no rules and makes the tile itself the cell a `divider` grid separates.

props.name: title
props.doc: The caption's run-in lead, naming what the panel above it shows.

props.name: description
props.doc: The sentence continuing the caption after the lead; overridden by the default slot.

props.name: src
props.doc: URL of the tile's media image; ignored when the `media` slot is filled.

props.name: alt
props.doc: Alternative text describing what the image shows; empty keeps it decorative.

props.name: padded
props.doc: Inset the media — inside the frame in the `frame` register, from the cell's edges in `plain`. Turn it off for an asset that should run to the cell's edges; the caption keeps its own inset either way.

props.name: fluid
props.doc: Stretch the media to the frame's full width with its aspect ratio locked, so it grows and shrinks with the tile; off, slotted media keeps its own size, centred.

props.name: mediaScale
props.doc: Scale of the media inside its frame, around its centre. The frame keeps its size and clips whatever grows past it, so a scene drawn small on its canvas can be fitted to the tile without changing the band's rhythm.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: The caption body after the lead; replaces the `description` prop.

slots.name: media
slots.notes: The scene the frame holds; replaces the `src` image.

media-tile.purpose: One cell of a media band: a scene above, and under it a run-in caption whose lead names what the scene shows and whose sentence continues on the same line, so a row of tiles reads as one paragraph of claims under one row of panels. It comes in two registers. `frame` draws the page's frame language around the media alone — never around the copy — which is what lets the captions sit on the page column with no rules between them. `plain` draws no rules at all: the tile is itself the cell, filled and inset, for a `card-grid` in its `divider` register where the grid's own hairlines separate the columns.
useWhen: For a row of three or four scenes that each need one sentence of explanation, laid out by `card-grid` in its `gap` register (`frame`) or its `divider` register (`plain`).
When the claim is a label for the picture above it (`AI workloads.`, `Middleware.`) rather than a section heading in its own right.
When the media should carry the page's frame language — hairline rules and corner marks — and the copy should not (`frame`).
For a full-bleed band whose columns are separated by the grid's own hairlines, where a frame per cell would double every rule (`plain`).
avoidWhen: When the claim deserves a heading and a place in the document outline → use `topic`, which leads with a real `h2`/`h3`.
When the tile is a padded surface card with a glyph and a link → use `topic` in a `CardGrid.Cell`.
For one scene beside a block of copy across the full band → use `media-split`.
For a mosaic whose cells claim different numbers of columns → use `bento-grid`.
For the grid that lays the tiles out, or a framed cell that wraps media *and* copy together → use `card-grid`.
related: card-grid` — the grid that lays a row of tiles out; use its `gap` register, whose gutters keep every tile's frame its own.
topic` — the heading-led claim, for a band whose items belong in the outline.
media-split` — one scene beside one block of copy, across the whole band.
frame-box` — the frame this tile draws around its media.
illustration` — the scene the frame usually holds; unnamed, it renders the placeholder that reserves a tile's space.
bestPractices: End the lead with a full stop. It runs into the sentence that follows it, so the stop is what separates them — the component adds no punctuation of its own.
Keep the lead to one or two words. It is a label for the panel above it, and a long lead swallows the first line of the sentence.
Give every tile in a band a caption of roughly the same length. The frames are equalised by the grid row; ragged captions are what make a band look uneven.

Reach for `padded` off when the media is an exported asset that already carries its own air, or when it should run to the cell's edges so a list or a table reads as continuing past them. A composed scene wants the inset.

Pair the register with the grid. `frame` belongs in `card-grid`'s `gap` register, whose gutters keep every frame its own; the `divider` register would rule the captions as well as the panels. `plain` belongs in the `divider` register, where the grid draws every rule and the tile fills its own background so the gap has something to show through.
Do not put a `frame` tile in a `divider` grid. The grid's hairline and the frame's rule then sit a padding apart, and the band reads as two competing grids.

Turn `fluid` on for a band whose scenes share one frame size, so every tile renders its scene at the same zoom whatever the column width. Scenes on different frames come out at different zooms under `fluid` — fix the frames, not the tiles.

Reach for `mediaScale` when a scene sits small or large on its canvas — a cluster of icon boxes drawn at its own size on the 592×300 frame reads as a speck in a tile. Set it per tile, so each scene in a band reaches the same visual height, and keep it at or under the value where the scene's widest edge meets the frame; anything past that is clipped.
Leave the media slot empty while a scene is still being drawn: the frame holds the tile's floor height, so the band keeps its rhythm instead of collapsing.

The scene is an official `Illustration`, inset from the frame by the `padded` default. Type a URL into `src` in the Controls panel and the tile swaps the scene for a plain image; clear `description` and the caption is the lead alone, with the frame holding its height either way.

props.name: autoplay
props.doc: Advances to the next client on a timer; pauses under the pointer or keyboard focus, restarts its count on a selection, and never runs under reduced motion.

props.name: autoplayInterval
props.doc: Milliseconds each client is held before the band advances.

props.name: showProgress

slots.name: actions
slots.notes: A trailing control under the featured quotation's attribution, such as a secondary `Button` to the success stories; rendered in `quote`'s own `actions` area, the same for every client.

quote-tabs.purpose: A testimonial band a reader browses by client: the selected client's quotation featured at the top in the client's own colours, and a wall of client cards below it that is the selector itself — clicking a card brings that client's quotation in. It is the band a page reaches for when several customers have one strong sentence each and only one of them should be read at a time. The band owns the selection and nothing else. The featured quotation is `quote` in its `highlight` register, and every card is the same framed cell `logo-wall` draws, so a quotation and a client card look the same here as everywhere else on the page. The quotation travels sideways in the direction of the choice — a card later in the wall brings its quotation in from the right, an earlier one from the left — so the reader feels the wall as a sequence. Left alone it moves through the clients on its own, the way `media-tabs` does: a hairline along the panel's bottom edge fills toward the next client, and the band holds still while the reader points at it or works it from the keyboard.
useWhen: To feature one client quotation at a time out of three to twelve peers, with every other client one click away on the wall below.
As a success-story band where the wall of customers and the quotation are the same content, not two lists.
avoidWhen: For one quotation on its own → use `quote` with `kind="highlight"`.
For several quotations read side by side or swiped through → use `quote-carousel`.
For a wall whose cards link to each customer's story → use `logo-wall`.
For a moving strip of marks with no links → use `ticker`.
For switching a page's content between views → use `tabs`.
related: quote` — the `highlight` register this band renders for the selected client.
logo-wall` — the same framed client cells, as links out rather than as a selector.
card-grid` — the framed grid the cards are laid out on.
frame-box` — the registration frame the quotation panel is drawn in, with the same corner marks as the cards below it; also what a page wraps the band in to close its outer edges.
quote-carousel` — the same testimonials as a row the reader scrolls through, every one visible.
media-tabs` — the same timer and progress hairline, for claims paired with a medium.
bestPractices: Give the wall a full row: six clients fill it from `lg` up and three from below `sm`, so six or twelve leave no empty cell.

Give every item a `logo` in the client's own colours; it is drawn as-is on its card and in the featured quotation, so pick artwork that carries its own contrast on both themes. Without one, `mark` names a one-ink mark from the brand registry instead.

Let `clientName` default to the registry's label for `mark`; set it when the item has only a `logo`, or a client the registry does not carry. It is the card's accessible name, so it is never optional in practice.

Keep each quotation to one or two sentences, verbatim, without typed quotation marks — `quote` draws its own glyph. The panel holds the tallest quotation's height for all of them and floors the attribution and the `actions` control, so one much longer quotation opens a wide gap under every shorter one.
Keep each quotation readable inside `autoplayInterval`; raise the interval before shortening a verbatim quotation, and turn `autoplay` off when the band sits beside other moving content.

examples.name: Default
examples.summary: Six clients, one quotation on screen at a time. Left alone the band moves to the next client every five seconds, with an orange hairline filling along the panel’s bottom edge; pointing at the band or reaching it with `Tab` holds the quotation. Click a card, or focus the wall and use the arrow keys — `Tab` reaches only the selected card, `ArrowRight` and `ArrowLeft` move and select, wrapping at either end, and `Home` / `End` jump to the first and last client. A card later in the wall brings its quotation in from the right and sends the old one out to the left; an earlier card reverses it. The selected card sits on `--bg-selected`. Fourbank passes a registry `mark` instead of a `logo`, so it is drawn in the theme’s one ink.

headers/auth-header.name: AuthHeader
headers/auth-header.title: Templates/Headers/AuthHeader
headers/auth-header.summary: The console bar for the signed-out and onboarding screens: sign in, sign up, password recovery and the first-run steps. A `GlobalHeader` in its default `content` placement with the brand at the start and one outlined Documentation button at the end. There is no navigation, no search and no account control, because there is no session to act on yet. Built from `GlobalHeader`, `Button` and `Brand`.

headers/creation-header.name: CreationHeader
headers/creation-header.title: Templates/Headers/CreationHeader
headers/creation-header.summary: The console bar for the focused creation shell: create, edit and deploy flows that run without the navigation rail. A `GlobalHeader` in its default `content` placement, spanning the whole window. Start: a small back button, the brand and the breadcrumb of where the flow lives. End: the account avatar alone, so the signed-in user stays visible. The bar carries no search, Create or Agent: the flow is the one thing on screen. Every one-screen create page (SinglePageCreate), every stepped one (MultipageCreate), the creation wizards (SourceWizard, ProvisionWizard), the deploy flows and the CreateHub render it. The back button returns to the list the flow started from; the wizards drop it and the crumb once they reach the provisioning and success screens. Built from `GlobalHeader`, `Breadcrumb`, `IconButton`, `Avatar` and `Brand`.

variants.name: CreateHub
variants.summary: The Creation Center header: the back control returns Home and the crumb is the single current page.

variants.name: Terminal
variants.summary: A creation wizard once the last step is submitted: the provisioning and success screens keep only the brand and the avatar, with no back control and no crumb.

headers/docs-header.name: DocsHeader
headers/docs-header.title: Templates/Headers/DocsHeader
headers/docs-header.summary: The documentation bar: a `GlobalHeader` in its default `content` placement, so it runs full bleed across the window and opens on the page boundary. Start: the navigation trigger below `lg`, the brand with the Docs tag, and the section links from `lg`. End: search, GitHub, then Console. Search leads the end cluster in every channel, so it sits at the start of the buttons wherever the reader is. The sample widens the search into a field carrying the ⌘K shortcut once the bar is wide enough; the control is an icon button below that, and an icon button here. Built from `GlobalHeader`, `NavigationMenu`, `IconButton`, `Button` and `Brand`.

headers/resource-header.name: ResourceHeader
headers/resource-header.title: Templates/Headers/ResourceHeader
headers/resource-header.summary: The console bar for every page inside the persistent shell, at its first and second level of resource. A `GlobalHeader` in its default `content` placement, sitting in the content zone beside the navigation rail. Start: the navigation trigger below `md`, the brand, and the breadcrumb from the second level. End: search first, then Create, the Agent button and the account avatar. The first level of a resource names itself with its own page, so the bar carries the brand alone; the second level adds the module and the resource name as a breadcrumb. Below `md` the sample collapses Create and Agent into icon buttons, and from a bar width of `--container-2xl` it widens the search into a field with the ⌘K shortcut. Both thresholds are read from the theme tokens. Built from `GlobalHeader`, `Breadcrumb`, `IconButton`, `Button`, `ButtonHighlight`, `Avatar` and `Brand`.

variants.name: SecondLevel
variants.summary: A resource inside a module. The breadcrumb names the module and the resource, and shows from `md`; the last crumb is the current page and carries no link.

headers/site-header.name: SiteHeader
headers/site-header.title: Templates/Headers/SiteHeader
headers/site-header.summary: The marketing bar: a sticky `GlobalHeader` in its `site` placement. The surface runs to the window edges while the regions are capped at the bar’s own measure and centred, so the bar answers to the framed page under it. Start: the navigation trigger below `xl` and the brand. Middle: the navigation, from `xl`. End: Contact from `xl`, then Login and Start for free, with search last. The mega-menus and the navigation sheet are documented on Templates › Marketing › Shell › SiteNav. Built from `GlobalHeader`, `NavigationMenu`, `IconButton`, `Button` and `Brand`.

platform/account/change-plan-drawer.title: Templates/Platform/Account/ChangePlanDrawer
platform/account/change-plan-drawer.summary: The Change plan drawer the Billing page opens from its Subscription Plan card: a Monthly or Yearly switch over the Free, Pro and Enterprise `CardPricing` cards, each with its feature list and one action, on an account that is on Free. Continue with Pro opens the Upgrade to Pro drawer on top of it, and Contact sales closes it. Built from `Drawer`, `PanelHeader`, `PanelContent`, `ToggleGroup`, `CardPricing` and `Button`.

platform/account/onboarding-form.name: OnboardingForm
platform/account/onboarding-form.title: Templates/Platform/Account/OnboardingForm
platform/account/onboarding-form.summary: The /signup/onboarding screen, frame included: the signed-out `GlobalHeader` over a two-column grid whose left column is a `Card` with a flat `Progress`, the step counter and heading, the step’s fields and a Back / Continue row, and whose right column, from `lg` up, is a wireframe of the app the new organization will open into. The flow shows one step at a time; each story here is one of the three. Built from `Field` with `Input`, `RadioCards` under a `Label` with a `HelperText`, a `Field.Label` choice card around a `Switch`, `Tag`, `Avatar` and `Button`; picking a paid plan opens the upgrade `Drawer` with `ToggleGroup`, `Field` with `Input`, `Select` and `Checkbox`, `Link` and `Alert`.

platform/auth.name: Auth
platform/auth.title: Templates/Platform/Auth
platform/auth.summary: The signed-out screens of a platform app, frame included: a full-height page with the signed-out `GlobalHeader` (the product mark and a Documentation button) over a centred column that holds one `Card` and the prompt and terms under it. It serves /login, /signup and /signup/verify. The Google and GitHub buttons lead the card, over an “or” `Separator`. Each field is a required `Label` over `Input` or a `Field` with `PasswordInput` and `PasswordRequirements`; a `HelperText` appears only after the primary action, saying whether the field is empty or malformed. The rest is `Button`, `IconButton` in a `Tooltip`, a `Tag` and a `Alert`. Errors follow one rule: auth never toasts. Each error story is one endpoint response, and every outcome lands in the same small `Alert` at the top of the card, above the fields. What changes is the severity and what it carries: nothing after a 401, because the fields under it are the recovery; Retry when nobody can fix it (503, 500, timeout); the Sign in and reset-your-password links when the address is already registered (409). Built from `PageHeader`, `GlobalHeader`, `Tag`, `Card`, `Alert`, `Label`, `Input`, `Field`, `PasswordInput`, `PasswordRequirements`, `HelperText` and `Button`.

variants.name: ServiceUnavailable

variants.name: ServerError

variants.name: Timeout
variants.summary: No response: the same message as the 500 but warning, because the request may still have gone through, with Retry.

platform/create/create-in-drawer.name: CreateInDrawer
platform/create/create-in-drawer.title: Templates/Platform/Create/CreateInDrawer
platform/create/create-in-drawer.summary: The right-side form drawer every item created or edited inside a resource opens, such as a domain, a record, an environment, a variable or a rule: a panel header with the title, a muted one-line description and the close button; a disabled-while-saving fieldset of `Section` bands, each a heading with a `Hint` glyph over its stacked `Field` components; and one submit button in the footer that flags empty required fields only after it is pressed and shows its loading state while the save is in flight. Its state resets each time it opens, so the content stays in place while it closes. Add Domain opens from under Domains on the resource’s Settings tab, from a domain row menu to edit it, and from Add Environment in the resource environment menu. The Environment select lists every environment, says when choosing one connects it to the resource, and ends in a Create Environment option. Choosing Bring my own Domain drops the free-domain addon and reveals the Certificate select, preselecting a certificate that already covers the address. Built from `SettingsSection`, `Drawer` and its parts, `PanelHeader`, `PanelContent`, `PanelFooter`, `Field` (with `InputGroup` and `RadioButton` choice cards), `Label` and `HelperText` around `Select`, `NumberInput`, `Input`, `Textarea`, `Hint`, `Link`, `Alert` and `Button`. The same drawer comes in three more shapes, each a variant: ItemRows, a list page whose Create Service drawer groups `Item` rows under section-titled flush `Card`s; NestedDrawer, an Add Instance drawer whose Service select creates the missing service in a second, medium drawer stacked above it and selects it back; and DeploymentSettings, the drawer that creates a Deployment Setting from a Build & Deployment settings panel. The variants add `PageHeader`, `SettingRow`, the platform shell, `Card`, `Item` and `Switch`.

platform/create/deploy-drawer.name: DeployDrawer
platform/create/deploy-drawer.title: Templates/Platform/Create/DeployDrawer
platform/create/deploy-drawer.summary: The drawer a platform deploys from, opened by the outlined Deploy button on a service or a project. Every variant shares one Resources card: a row per resource with its Ready tag, the picked version and a Change Version popover, and a Dependencies disclosure with the modules and integrations the service references. On a service the default flow is environment first: the Project card uses an existing project or creates one, the environments come as radio blocks, and Projects Impacted lists every project the environment’s shared Deployment Settings publish to. A deploy started without a pinned version first builds one, so the drawer opens as Build and Deployment with a Building row and the other sections faded. A service can also deploy project first, picking the project before the environment. On a project, the drawer carries every resource it serves and warns when its Deployment Settings also publish elsewhere. Built from `SettingsSection`, `Drawer`, the `Panel` parts, `Card`, `Item`, `Accordion`, `Separator`, `Popover`, `DropdownMenu`, `ToggleGroup`, `Field` choice cards with `RadioButton`, `Input`, `Avatar`, `Tag`, `Hint`, `Spinner`, `Alert`, `Tooltip` and `Button`.

Without a Git provider the step is the Connect a Git provider card; once one is connected it is the Deploy your project form, with the scope and the repository name with its privacy switch side by side over the template settings, and the Deploy button that stays disabled until every required setting is filled. Deploying hands the same column to the build logs (the DeploymentFlow template) and then to the success screen (the DeploySuccess template). Import from Git and Upload a Project reach the same page with the form trimmed to the repository or the uploaded files. Built from `GlobalHeader`, `Breadcrumb`, `Card`, `EmptyState`, `Field`, `Select`, `Label`, `InputGroup`, `Switch`, `Input` and `Button`.

platform/create/deployment-flow.name: DeploymentFlow
platform/create/deployment-flow.title: Templates/Platform/Create/DeploymentFlow
platform/create/deployment-flow.summary: The deploy flow card a create flow streams while it deploys: a Card titled Deployment whose header carries the run status, a StatusIndicator while it runs and the Phased or Complete ToggleGroup once it has failed, opening on a cloning splash and then streaming the DeploymentLogs block with its controls moved up to that header: a Logs row with the step count, the pipeline as an Accordion of steps, each with its status glyph, its time and its own LogView, over a flush Progress. A create flow that provisions rather than deploys titles it Provisioning, with a Creating status and a Provisioning splash; the standalone logs block is the DeploymentLogs template. The live stream is shown here as one story per state, with the steps and log lines of the template deploy pipeline. variants.name: Running

variants.summary: The last line has printed: every step checked and collapsed, a Completed Tag in the Logs row and the progress bar retired, a beat before the flow hands over to its success screen.

variants.name: Failed
variants.summary: The routing rules were rejected: that step is open on its error output with a Failed Tag, the steps behind it read Skipped, and the header swaps the status for the Phased or Complete switch.
